name: Formation of the Earth
summary: The Earth formed approximately 4.54 billion years ago by accretion of material from the solar nebula.
body:
Earth formed about **4.54 billion years ago** out of the disc of dust and gas left over from the Sun's formation. Successively larger fragments of that material collided and stuck together until a planet-sized body had assembled, most of it within about 10 to 20 million years. The heat released left the surface molten, and the planet sorted itself into a metallic core and a rocky mantle.

Iron and other heavy metals sank towards the centre in an episode sometimes called the iron catastrophe, within roughly ten million years of the start of accretion; lighter silicates rose to form the mantle and the earliest crust. Core formation gave the planet a magnetic field. That first crust was repeatedly destroyed and remade, and no rock of it survives anywhere.

The age is established by radiometric dating rather than by any surviving terrestrial rock. Meteorites that never melted preserve the age of the solar system's first solids, about 4.567 billion years; the oldest terrestrial material of any kind is detrital zircon from Western Australia at about 4.4 billion years. The conventional figure for Earth itself carries an uncertainty of around one per cent.

Within the first hundred million years a Mars-sized body struck the growing planet, and the debris became [the Moon](event:theia-impact). Gases released from the interior, together with water most likely delivered by asteroidal material, condensed into [the first oceans](event:first-oceans). The Hadean eon, which covers this whole interval, ended about 4 billion years ago.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Earth).

name: Giant impact forms the Moon
summary: A Mars-sized body, Theia, collided with the proto-Earth; debris from the impact coalesced into the Moon.
body:
The giant-impact hypothesis is the standard explanation for the Moon's origin. A protoplanet about the size of Mars, named Theia, struck [the proto-Earth](event:earth-formation) roughly 4.5 billion years ago, between about 20 and 100 million years after the solar system formed, with several recent estimates clustering nearer 4.45 billion. Material vaporised and thrown into orbit by the collision re-accumulated as the Moon.

Three lines of evidence support it. The Earth–Moon system carries an anomalously high angular momentum, which a glancing impact would supply. The Moon has only a small iron core, as expected if it formed largely from mantle material while Theia's core sank into Earth. And lunar and terrestrial rocks have stable-isotope ratios identical to within measurement error, which points to a common origin.

That last point is also the hypothesis's main difficulty. A simple impact model predicts that the Moon should be built mostly from the impactor and should therefore differ isotopically from Earth. Models that mix the two bodies more thoroughly, or that begin with a faster-spinning proto-Earth, are attempts to resolve it; the abundance of water and of volatile elements in lunar basalts is a further open question.

The aftermath left Earth spinning with a day of about five hours, which tides have since slowed, and the Moon much closer than it is now. The Moon's pull has kept Earth's axial tilt from wandering as widely as it otherwise would.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant-impact_hypothesis).

name: Origin of life
summary: Self-replicating chemical systems emerged, likely around hydrothermal vents, forming the first cellular life.
body:
Abiogenesis is the natural process by which living systems arose from non-living chemistry. It is understood not as a single event but as a sequence of steps of increasing complexity: the synthesis of organic molecules, the appearance of self-replicating polymers, and the enclosure of that chemistry within a membrane. The geological record places the transition between roughly 4.3 and 3.5 billion years ago.

The earliest claimed physical evidence, putative microbialites in the Nuvvuagittuq greenstone belt of Quebec, possibly 4.28 billion years old, is disputed. Biogenic graphite in 3.7-billion-year-old metasedimentary rocks from Greenland, identified by its depleted carbon-13 content, is more widely accepted, and the 3.48-billion-year-old [stromatolites](event:stromatolites) of the Dresser Formation in Western Australia are the oldest structures most researchers accept as built by life.

Several hypotheses compete over the setting and the chemistry. The RNA world proposes an early phase in which RNA both carried information and catalysed reactions, before DNA and proteins divided those roles between them. Submarine alkaline hydrothermal vents are a favoured environment because they maintain a continuous chemical disequilibrium between hydrogen-rich fluid and carbon dioxide dissolved in seawater. The Miller–Urey experiment of 1952 showed that amino acids form spontaneously from simple gases under prebiotic conditions, though the strongly reducing atmosphere it assumed is no longer thought to be the right one.

Every organism alive descends from a single ancestral population, the last universal common ancestor. Reconstructions from genes shared across the tree of life describe it as already complex: anaerobic, dependent on the Wood–Ljungdahl pathway for fixing carbon, and living in a hydrothermal setting. It was not the first life, only the one lineage whose descendants survive.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abiogenesis).

name: Oxygenic photosynthesis evolves
summary: Cyanobacteria evolved the ability to split water molecules using light energy, producing free oxygen as a byproduct.
body:
Cyanobacteria evolved a form of photosynthesis that splits water to obtain electrons and releases oxygen as waste. The oxygen it released changed the composition of Earth's atmosphere, and every plant and alga performs it today using chloroplasts descended from cyanobacteria taken up as endosymbionts.

Splitting water demands a far stronger oxidant than earlier [anoxygenic pathways](event:anoxygenic-photosynthesis) needed. It is achieved by linking two photosystems in series and by a manganese cluster that strips electrons from water molecules four at a time. What it buys is an inexhaustible electron donor: unlike hydrogen sulphide or dissolved iron, water is everywhere.

When this happened is not settled. Geological evidence puts oxygenic photosynthesis in place by at least 2.45 to 2.32 billion years ago; arguments from biomarkers and molecular clocks for cyanobacteria at 2.7 or even 3.5 billion years are contested. Atmospheric oxygen nonetheless stayed at or below about a thousandth of a per cent of today's level until 2.4 billion years ago, because the oxygen produced was consumed as fast as it was made, by dissolved iron, by volcanic gases and by reduced minerals at the surface.

Once those sinks were exhausted, oxygen accumulated: the [Great Oxidation Event](event:great-oxidation).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyanobacteria).

name: Great Oxidation Event
summary: Free oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere for the first time, proving toxic to most existing life and oxidising iron across the planet's surface.
body:
The Great Oxidation Event was the first accumulation of free oxygen in Earth's atmosphere and shallow seas, beginning about 2.46 to 2.43 billion years ago. Oxygen made by [cyanobacteria](event:oxygenic-photosynthesis) had been consumed for hundreds of millions of years by dissolved iron, volcanic gases and reduced minerals; once those sinks could no longer keep up, it began to build up in the air.

Oxygen destroyed atmospheric methane, a far stronger greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide, and the loss of that warming is the standard explanation for [the Huronian glaciation](event:huronian-glaciation). It was lethal to most of the anaerobic life then existing, and one estimate puts the resulting reduction of the biosphere at around eighty per cent. It also made aerobic respiration possible, which extracts far more energy per unit of food than fermentation, and it built an ozone layer. By reacting with rock at the surface it more than doubled the number of mineral species on Earth, adding some 2,500 varieties.

Oxygen did not simply rise and stay. It overshot in the middle of the event and then fell back, and the atmosphere held only around a tenth of its modern oxygen content by the end. It stayed near that level for more than a billion years afterwards, until the [Neoproterozoic oxygenation](event:tonian-oxygenation). The phases are set out in the steps.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Oxidation_Event).

steps.name: Oxygen begins to accumulate
steps.page:
Sulphur isotopes in sedimentary rocks record the disappearance of mass-independent fractionation, a signature that can only be produced when the atmosphere is essentially free of oxygen and ultraviolet light reaches sulphur dioxide unshielded. Its loss, between about 2.46 and 2.43 billion years ago, is the sharpest marker of the transition, and it is what dates the event.

Oxygen levels at this stage were still tiny by modern standards, but enough to change how iron, sulphur and manganese behaved at the Earth's surface, and enough to begin destroying atmospheric methane.

steps.name: Lomagundi–Jatuli excursion
steps.page:
The largest and longest positive carbon-isotope excursion in the geological record, registered in carbonate rocks on several continents. A carbonate signature this heavy implies that organic carbon was being buried on an enormous scale, and burying organic carbon is what leaves oxygen behind. Estimates of atmospheric oxygen during the excursion run as high as modern levels.

It is the high-water mark of the event rather than its steady state: the excursion ends, and the isotopic record swings back.

steps.name: Return to low oxygen
steps.page:
The Lomagundi excursion is followed by a sharp reversal associated with the deposition of vast volumes of organic-rich black shale, known as the Shunga–Francevillian event. Oxygen production could not be sustained at the earlier rate once the nutrients supporting it had been drawn down, and atmospheric oxygen fell back to a low level.

It stayed there for most of the next billion and a half years, an interval sometimes called the boring billion, until the [Tonian oxygenation](event:tonian-oxygenation) began to raise it again.

name: First eukaryotic cells
summary: A cell engulfed another cell, retaining it as an internal organelle; this established the compartmented eukaryotic cell with mitochondria.
body:
Eukaryotes are organisms whose cells keep their DNA inside a membrane-bound nucleus. Every animal, plant, fungus and alga is one, along with a great many single-celled organisms. The lineage arose when an archaeon took up a bacterium and kept it: that bacterium became the mitochondrion, and the merger is the defining event of eukaryogenesis.

Genomic work places the host among the Asgard archaea and the endosymbiont among the alphaproteobacteria. A second, later merger, this time with a cyanobacterium, produced chloroplasts, and with them the whole photosynthetic side of the eukaryotes, the algae and eventually the land plants. Both organelles still carry small genomes of their own and divide independently of the cell around them.

Dating the origin is difficult. Fossils that can be assigned confidently to living eukaryotic groups appear about 1.2 billion years ago, with red algae among the earliest. Older candidates exist, such as organic-walled microfossils from the Ruyang Group in China, 1.8 to 1.6 billion years old, but their affinities are uncertain, and molecular clocks generally give older dates than the fossils do.

The last eukaryotic common ancestor was a population rather than an individual, and it already had a nucleus, a flagellum, aerobic mitochondria and the machinery of [sexual reproduction](event:sexual-reproduction). What compartmentalisation and mitochondria bought was energy available per gene, which is the usual explanation for why this lineage alone produced large, complex [multicellular](event:multicellular-eukaryotes) bodies.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eukaryote).

name: Snowball Earth
summary: Glaciers advanced toward the equator, possibly covering the entire ocean surface, during the Cryogenian period.
body:
Snowball Earth is the hypothesis that the planet froze from the poles almost or entirely to the equator during the Cryogenian period, between about 717 and 635 million years ago. Two glaciations are involved: the Sturtian, roughly 717 to 660 million years ago, and the Marinoan, roughly 650 to 635. Each lasted for tens of millions of years, far longer than any later ice age.

The evidence is geological. Glacial deposits of this age are found on nearly every continent, and palaeomagnetic measurements place some of them (in Svalbard, Greenland and Australia) at tropical latitudes at the time. Dropstones released from floating ice sit embedded in marine sediments. Above the glacial rocks lie distinctive layers of carbonate, tens of metres thick and deposited very rapidly; these cap carbonates are read as the product of intense chemical weathering under a carbon-dioxide-rich atmosphere immediately after the ice melted. [Banded iron formations](event:banded-iron-formations-peak) briefly reappear, which requires an ocean that had gone anoxic beneath a lid of ice.

The usual account of how it began involves large volcanic provinces erupting in the wet tropics as [Rodinia](event:rodinia) broke apart: weathering the fresh basalt drew down carbon dioxide, cooling produced ice, and ice reflected sunlight, cooling the planet further. Ending it required volcanic carbon dioxide to accumulate for millions of years beneath the ice until the greenhouse effect overwhelmed the albedo, after which deglaciation would have been very fast.

A weaker version, the slushball, keeps a belt of open or thin ice around the equator. Some sedimentary structures indicate moving ice and open water, and climate models have difficulty freezing the whole ocean without altering other assumptions. Either way the episodes end immediately before the appearance of the [Ediacaran biota](event:ediacaran) and, a little later, the [Cambrian explosion](event:cambrian-explosion).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowball_Earth).

name: Cambrian explosion
summary: Nearly all modern animal body plans appeared in the fossil record within a period of tens of millions of years.
body:
The Cambrian explosion was an interval beginning about 538.8 million years ago during which most major animal groups appear in the fossil record for the first time. Within roughly 13 to 25 million years, animals with hard parts, jointed limbs, eyes and predatory habits are present in marine sediments worldwide, where before there had been little but microbes, algae and the soft-bodied [Ediacaran biota](event:ediacaran).

Three deposits of exceptional preservation carry most of what is known. The Chengjiang fauna of Yunnan and Sirius Passet in northern Greenland are early Cambrian; the [Burgess Shale](event:burgess-shale-fauna) of British Columbia is about 508 million years old. All three preserve soft tissue, which ordinary fossilisation destroys, and so record animals that would otherwise be invisible.

No single cause is agreed. Rising oxygen would have permitted larger and more active bodies. The appearance of predation could have set off an arms race between armour and the means of breaking it, though predators existed before the Cambrian. Changes in the developmental genes that govern body plans, particularly the Hox genes, allow large morphological changes to follow from small genetic ones. Higher calcium concentrations in seawater would have made mineralised skeletons cheaper to build.

How sudden it really was is also disputed. Molecular clocks put the divergence of the major animal lineages well back into the Neoproterozoic, and trace fossils show bilaterian animals moving through sediment before the Cambrian. Some researchers argue that the radiation was no faster than others in animal history, and that its apparent abruptness owes much to the sudden preservability of skeletons and to the incompleteness of the earlier record.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambrian_explosion).

name: Plants colonise the land
summary: Spore-bearing plants colonized terrestrial environments, beginning the development of continental vegetation.
body:
Plants moved onto land in the middle Ordovician, around 470 million years ago. The first evidence is not of plants themselves but of their spores: cryptospores with tough sporopollenin walls, recovered from Ordovician rocks in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere on Gondwana, comparable to those produced by living liverworts.

Land plants descend from freshwater green algae, from among the charophytes, the group modern stoneworts belong to. The move demanded solutions to desiccation, structural support and the transport of water, and these arrived over the following hundred million years rather than at once. Simple conducting cells appear in the Silurian; true vascular tissue with lignin-strengthened walls, which resists collapse under tension, follows, and *Cooksonia* from the later Silurian is the earliest known vascular plant. Roots developed gradually through the Devonian, from rhizoids a few millimetres deep to systems reaching nearly a metre. Broad leaves became common around 360 million years ago, once falling carbon dioxide made a large light-gathering surface worth its cost in water.

The consequences for the planet were large. Roots broke up rock and acidified soils, deepening chemical weathering and drawing down carbon dioxide; sediment began to be retained on land, and mudrock becomes markedly more common in the record from the Ordovician onward. [Animals followed the vegetation](event:silurian-land-colonisation) ashore, and by the Carboniferous plants had built [forests](event:carboniferous-forests) dense enough to bury carbon on a global scale.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolutionary_history_of_plants).

name: Ordovician–Silurian extinction
summary: Approximately 85% of marine species went extinct as glaciation locked up seawater and drained the shallow continental shelves.
body:
The Late Ordovician mass extinction, about 445 to 443 million years ago, was the first of the five largest extinctions in the fossil record and the second largest by proportion of genera lost. Between 49 and 60 per cent of marine genera and close to 85 per cent of marine species disappeared. Life was still almost entirely marine, so the event is recorded only in the sea.

It came in two pulses. The first, at the Katian–Hirnantian boundary, coincides with the rapid growth of an ice sheet over Gondwana, which then lay across the South Pole. The world shifted from greenhouse to icehouse within a geologically short time; sea level fell, draining the shallow continental shelves where most life lived, and water temperatures dropped faster than warm-adapted species could tolerate.

The second pulse came in the late Hirnantian as the glaciation ended. Rising sea level was accompanied by widespread anoxia and euxinia (oxygen-depleted, sulphidic water), which spread across the shelves and persisted into the early Silurian.

Brachiopods, bryozoans, [trilobites](event:trilobite-diversification), conodonts, echinoderms, corals and graptolites were all heavily affected, and the [reef ecosystems](event:ordovician-reef-ecosystems) of the period were dismantled. Unlike later extinctions it eliminated few whole groups: the fauna that recovered through the Silurian was much the same one, at lower diversity.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Ordovician_mass_extinction).

name: Vertebrates walk on land
summary: Lobe-finned fish with weight-bearing limbs, exemplified by Tiktaalik, moved onto land.
body:
Tetrapods, four-limbed vertebrates including all amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals, evolved from lobe-finned fish during the Devonian. Their origin is among the best-documented major transitions in the fossil record, though the sequence is less tidy than it once appeared.

The oldest evidence is a set of trackways at Zachełmie in Poland, made about 390 million years ago by an animal walking on limbs with digits. Fragmentary body fossils of *Elginerpeton* from Scotland and *Obruchevichthys* from Latvia follow at around 380 million years, though not everyone accepts them as tetrapods. Nearly complete skeletons appear late in the Devonian: *Acanthostega* and *Ichthyostega* from East Greenland, which had limbs with digits (eight of them on *Acanthostega*) but also internal gills and a tail fin.

*Tiktaalik roseae*, found on Ellesmere Island in the Canadian Arctic in 2004 and about 375 million years old, is a lobe-finned fish rather than a tetrapod: a flattened skull, a neck, and fin skeletons robust enough to prop the body up. It postdates the Polish trackways, which is the main reason the transition is now thought to have begun earlier than the body fossils by themselves would suggest.

These animals were aquatic, and limbs appear to have evolved for moving through shallow, weed-choked water rather than for walking on land. Fully terrestrial tetrapods, with the [amniotic egg](event:amniotic-egg) to free them from standing water, are a Carboniferous development.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrapod).

name: Pangaea supercontinent
summary: Nearly all continental landmasses united into a single supercontinent surrounded by the Panthalassic Ocean.
body:
Pangaea was a supercontinent that assembled during the Carboniferous, around 335 million years ago, and began to break apart at the end of the Triassic, about 200 million years ago. It brought nearly all of the world's continental crust into one mass, surrounded by a single superocean, Panthalassa, with the Tethys opening into it from the east.

Its existence is why the same Permian and Triassic land fossils (*Glossopteris*, *Lystrosaurus*, *Mesosaurus*, *Cynognathus*) are found on continents now separated by oceans, an argument Alfred Wegener made in 1912 and which was accepted only after seafloor spreading was demonstrated in the 1960s. Matching mountain belts and rock sequences across the Atlantic point the same way.

A single landmass has little coastline for its area, and the interior of Pangaea was consequently very dry: one of the most extensive desert systems in Earth's history occupied it, with short rainy seasons even well inland. The loss of shallow continental shelf, where most marine life lives, is among the background stresses often invoked for the severity of the [end-Permian extinction](event:permian-extinction).

Breakup came in three phases. Rifting between North America and Africa began in the Triassic and had opened the central [Atlantic](event:atlantic-opening) by about 175 million years ago. Gondwana came apart from the Early Cretaceous, separating Africa, South America, India, Antarctica and Australia. Finally, in the early Cenozoic, Laurentia parted from Eurasia and the Norwegian Sea opened, 60 to 55 million years ago. The continents are still moving.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea).

name: Permian–Triassic extinction
summary: Approximately 81% of marine species and 70% of land vertebrates went extinct in Earth's most severe biotic crisis.
body:
The Permian–Triassic extinction, about 252 million years ago, was the most severe biotic crisis in the fossil record, and is sometimes called the Great Dying. Around 81 per cent of marine species and some 70 per cent of terrestrial vertebrate species disappeared, along with 57 per cent of families and 62 per cent of genera. Precise dating of the boundary beds in South China places the main extinction between 251.941 and 251.880 million years ago, a window of roughly sixty thousand years.

The accepted cause is the eruption of the [Siberian Traps](event:siberian-traps), one of the largest volcanic events known. Magma intruded thick sequences of coal, carbonate and evaporite in the Tunguska basin and cooked them, so that the eruptions released far more carbon and halogen gas than the lava alone would have. Atmospheric carbon dioxide rose from roughly 400 to 2,500 parts per million and global temperature by around 8 °C. The oceans warmed, acidified and lost their oxygen; large areas became euxinic, charged with hydrogen sulphide. Ozone depletion and acid rain are also invoked.

Eight or nine orders of insects vanished, the only mass extinction that seriously affected them. [Trilobites](event:trilobite-diversification) ended here, as did the eurypterids and most of the range of form among crinoids, brachiopods and ammonoids. Around 93 per cent of foraminifera died. Reefs disappeared for millions of years. On land the [synapsids](event:synapsid-domination) that had dominated the Permian were reduced to a handful of surviving lines.

Recovery was slow and uneven. Some local marine communities were re-established within one or two million years and marine ecosystems were functioning again by the Middle Triassic, but terrestrial vertebrate faunas took around thirty million years to regain their complexity, and global marine diversity far longer. The depleted world of the Early Triassic is the one in which the [first dinosaurs](event:first-dinosaurs) appeared.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permian%E2%80%93Triassic_extinction_event).

name: First dinosaurs
summary: Small bipedal archosaurs from what is now Argentina mark the origin of the dinosaurian lineage.
body:
Dinosaurs originated in the Middle to Late Triassic, roughly twenty million years after the [end-Permian extinction](event:permian-extinction). The oldest substantial fossils come from the Ischigualasto Formation in north-western Argentina, dated to 231–230 million years ago, and from rocks of similar age in Brazil and Zimbabwe. *Herrerasaurus* and *Eoraptor* from Ischigualasto were bipedal and lightly built.

They were a minor part of Triassic land faunas, which were dominated by other archosaurs (the crocodile-line pseudosuchians), together with surviving [synapsids](event:synapsid-domination) and large amphibians. What distinguished dinosaurs anatomically was a hip socket open at its centre and a thigh bone with an inturned head, giving limbs held directly beneath the body rather than sprawling.

Their rise was a consequence of the [end-Triassic extinction](event:triassic-extinction) 201.4 million years ago, which removed most of the competing archosaur groups. Dinosaurs then dominated terrestrial ecosystems for the next 135 million years, through the Jurassic and the Cretaceous, reaching sizes no land animal has matched before or since.

The non-avian lineages ended at the [Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary](event:kpg-extinction) 66 million years ago. [Birds](event:first-birds), which are themselves dinosaurs, did not.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosaur).

name: Chicxulub impact
summary: A 10-kilometre-diameter asteroid impacted the Yucatán platform, releasing energy equivalent to billions of Hiroshima bombs.
body:
Part of [Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction](event:kpg-extinction). The Chicxulub crater lies buried beneath the northern Yucatán Peninsula and the sea floor off it, centred near the town of Chicxulub Puerto. It is 180 to 200 kilometres across and about a kilometre below younger sediment, and it was made 66 million years ago by an asteroid roughly ten kilometres in diameter, most probably a carbonaceous chondrite from beyond Jupiter's orbit.

Estimates of the energy released span two orders of magnitude, from tens of millions to billions of megatonnes of TNT equivalent, with winds above 1,000 kilometres an hour near the site. What made it globally lethal, however, was the target: the platform is thick carbonate and sulphur-rich gypsum, and vaporising them injected carbon dioxide and enormous quantities of sulphate aerosol into the stratosphere, where they blocked sunlight and later fell as acid rain.

It was found by accident. Glen Penfield and Antonio Camargo identified a buried circular magnetic and gravity anomaly during petroleum exploration in 1978, and their interpretation went largely unnoticed until Alan Hildebrand made contact in 1990; drill samples containing shock-metamorphic minerals confirmed it, and the identification was published in 1991. In 2016 a joint expedition drilled the offshore peak ring to 1,335 metres below the sea floor, recovering rock that had been fluidised by the impact and thrown back inward.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicxulub_crater).

name: Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction
summary: Approximately 75% of all species, including all non-avian dinosaurs, went extinct during a geologically brief interval.
body:
The Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction, 66 million years ago, ended the Mesozoic era and killed about three-quarters of the plant and animal species on Earth. All non-avian dinosaurs died, along with the pterosaurs, the mosasaurs and plesiosaurs, the ammonites and most of the calcareous plankton. Almost no land animal heavier than about 25 kilograms survived.

The cause is the impact of an asteroid at [Chicxulub](event:chicxulub) on the Yucatán platform. The first evidence was chemical: a thin clay layer at the boundary, found worldwide, containing far more iridium than Earth's crust normally holds but about as much as a meteorite. Shocked quartz, glass spherules and then a crater of the right age and size followed.

The immediate mechanism was the loss of sunlight. Dust and sulphate aerosols from vaporised rock spread through the stratosphere and shut down photosynthesis for months to years, collapsing food chains on land and in the surface ocean. Wildfires, a pulse of acid rain and megatsunamis exceeding a hundred metres in shallow seas added to it. The [Deccan Traps](event:deccan-traps) were erupting at the same time and had already been altering the climate, though modelling now assigns them a secondary role.

Survival was selective in ways that make sense of that mechanism. Small burrowing and semi-aquatic animals came through better than large surface-dwelling ones, and freshwater communities, which run on detritus rather than on living plants, did far better than terrestrial and marine ones dependent on photosynthesis. Among tetrapods the survivors were [birds](event:first-birds), crocodilians, turtles, lizards, snakes, amphibians and [mammals](event:paleocene-mammal-radiation).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous%E2%80%93Paleogene_extinction_event).

name: First stone tools
summary: Hominins began deliberately producing stone cutting tools, initiating the archaeological record.
body:
The deliberate flaking of stone to make cutting edges is where the archaeological record begins. The oldest claimed tools come from Lomekwi 3, west of Lake Turkana in Kenya, and are dated to 3.3 million years ago; they are large and heavy, struck by techniques unlike what follows, and whether they represent a tradition continuous with later toolmaking has not been established.

The first widespread industry is the Oldowan, which now reaches back to about 2.9 million years ago at Nyayanga in Kenya, with well-known assemblages from Gona in Ethiopia at 2.6 million and from Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, where Louis Leakey found the first examples in the 1930s. The technique is simple (a few flakes struck from a cobble with a hammerstone), but the flakes cut well, and the cores were used too.

Who made them is unsettled. They are conventionally attributed to early *Homo*, but the oldest examples predate the genus, and *Australopithecus garhi* and *Paranthropus* have both been proposed. More than one lineage may have been making them.

What the tools gave access to was meat and, by breaking bones, marrow, foods rich in energy and otherwise very hard for a primate to obtain. Cut-marked bones appear alongside them, and the change in diet is generally connected to the later increase in brain size. The [Acheulean hand-axe](event:hand-axe-tool-tradition) follows about 1.76 million years ago.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oldowan).

name: Quaternary ice ages begin
summary: Northern hemisphere ice sheets advanced and retreated repeatedly on orbital time scales.
body:
The Quaternary glaciation began 2.58 million years ago and is still in progress: the present is an interglacial within it, not a time outside it. Northern hemisphere ice sheets have grown and collapsed repeatedly through the period, while Antarctica has stayed glaciated throughout.

The rhythm is set by variations in Earth's orbit, the Milankovitch cycles. Eccentricity varies on a period near 100,000 years, axial tilt between about 22 and 24.5 degrees on 41,000 years, and precession on roughly 26,000. None of these changes the total sunlight the Earth receives by much; what they change is its distribution across seasons and latitudes, and what matters is whether northern summers are cool enough to leave the previous winter's snow unmelted.

For the first million and a half years the cycles followed the 41,000-year tilt period. After the Mid-Pleistocene Transition, about a million years ago, they lengthened to roughly 100,000 years and grew much larger in amplitude, for reasons still debated. Eight complete cycles have run in the last 740,000 years.

At their maxima the ice sheets were at least four kilometres thick and sea level stood about 120 metres lower than today. They ground down and rebuilt the landscapes of northern Europe, Canada and Siberia, and left millions of lakes behind them, among them the Great Lakes and the Baltic. The whole of hominin evolution and dispersal has taken place within this climate regime.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternary_glaciation).

name: Control of fire
summary: Hominins developed the ability to produce and maintain fire, affecting diet, safety, and social organisation.
body:
The control of fire gave early humans cooked food, warmth, protection from predators and light after dark. When it began is among the harder questions in palaeoanthropology, because the traces fire leaves are easily produced by natural burning and easily destroyed.

The earliest claims are contested. Burnt bone and ashed plant material from Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, found deep inside the cave and identified by micromorphology and infrared spectroscopy, are dated between about 1.8 and 1.0 million years ago. Reddened sediment at Koobi Fora in Kenya, consistent with heating to 200–400 °C, is around 1.5 million years old. Neither is universally accepted, and most evidence for controlled fire in the Lower Palaeolithic is regarded as uncertain.

Firmer evidence comes later. Gesher Benot Ya'aqov in Israel, about 780,000 years old, preserves repeatedly used hearth areas and burnt fish teeth in a pattern that indicates cooking. From 400,000 to 300,000 years ago hearths become common and unambiguous across Europe, western Asia and Africa; by around 125,000 years ago fire use is effectively universal among anatomically modern humans.

The cooking hypothesis holds that fire's main effect was nutritional: cooked food yields more usable energy for less chewing and less gut, which would help pay for a large brain. Critics point out that the archaeological timing fits the expansion of the brain poorly, and that fire's other benefits (warmth, protection from predators, light after dark) do not depend on cooking at all.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_of_fire_by_early_humans).

name: Origin of Homo sapiens
summary: Anatomically modern humans originated in Africa, with the oldest known fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco.
body:
*Homo sapiens* emerged in Africa at least 300,000 years ago. The oldest fossils generally assigned to the species come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco and are about 315,000 years old: the face is essentially modern, while the braincase is still long and low. Omo Kibish in Ethiopia, at about 233,000 years, provides the oldest anatomically modern skeleton, and Herto and Florisbad add further early material.

The picture that has replaced a single point of origin is a pan-African one. Different populations across the continent carried different combinations of modern and archaic features, and gene flow between them, over tens of thousands of years and thousands of kilometres, assembled the modern form, rather than any one lineage evolving it in isolation. The molecular evidence fits: the most recent common ancestor of living mitochondrial lineages dates to roughly 148,000 to 99,000 years ago and of Y chromosomes to 156,000 to 120,000, both long after the species itself appears.

Behavioural modernity (pigments, ornaments, composite tools, long-distance transport of raw material, systematic use of marine resources) accumulates over a long period, from perhaps 160,000 years ago onward, rather than arriving all at once.

Early excursions out of Africa are documented at Misliya Cave in Israel between 194,000 and 177,000 years ago and at Skhul and Qafzeh between 120,000 and 100,000, with a contested claim at Apidima in Greece around 210,000. None of those populations left descendants. The [dispersal that populated the world](event:out-of-africa) came later, between about 70,000 and 50,000 years ago, and by then *Homo sapiens* shared the planet with [Neanderthals](event:neanderthals), [Denisovans](event:denisovans) and at least two other human species.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_sapiens).

name: Out of Africa dispersal
summary: Modern humans dispersed from Africa and colonized every habitable continent within tens of thousands of years.
body:
The dispersal out of Africa is the expansion, between about 70,000 and 50,000 years ago, that put modern humans on every habitable continent. Every population living outside Africa today descends from it. The founding group was small (genetic evidence points to a few thousand people at most, carrying mitochondrial haplogroup L3), and it most probably crossed at the southern end of the Red Sea, at Bab-el-Mandeb, or overland through Sinai.

It was not the first attempt. Modern humans reached the Levant at Misliya Cave 194,000 to 177,000 years ago and at Skhul and Qafzeh 120,000 to 100,000 years ago, and there are early finds in Arabia and possibly Greece. None of those populations left descendants in the modern gene pool.

Along the way the dispersing population met and interbred with the archaic humans already in Eurasia. About 2 per cent of the genome of every non-African alive today is [Neanderthal](event:neanderthals), from admixture dated between roughly 65,000 and 47,000 years ago, and [Denisovan](event:denisovans) ancestry runs from 0.2 per cent in mainland Asia to around 5 per cent in New Guinea and Aboriginal Australia.

The expansion was rapid. [Australia](event:sahul) was reached by 65,000 to 50,000 years ago, across open water; Europe by 45,000; Siberia by 40,000 and the Russian Arctic by 27,000; and [the Americas](event:americas-peopling), the last continents, by about 16,000 years ago. The steps below follow that sequence.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_human_migrations).

steps.name: Crossing into Eurasia
steps.page:
A population carrying mitochondrial haplogroup L3 leaves north-east Africa, most probably by way of the Bab-el-Mandeb strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, where the crossing is narrowest and sea level during a glacial period stood far lower than today. An overland route through Sinai and the Levant is the alternative, and the two are not exclusive.

The genetic signal is of a founder group small enough that the whole of non-African humanity carries a subset of African variation. The route beyond the crossing is usually reconstructed as a southern one, along the coasts of Arabia, Iran and South Asia, which is also the fastest way to reach [Sahul](event:sahul).

steps.name: Arrival in Europe
steps.page:
Modern humans are securely present in Europe from about 45,000 years ago, with early sites in Bulgaria, Italy and Germany; some of the earliest individuals sequenced carry Neanderthal ancestry from interbreeding only a few generations back. They arrive into a continent occupied by [Neanderthals](event:neanderthals) and share it with them for several thousand years.

The Upper Palaeolithic industries belong to this period (blades struck from prepared cores, bone and antler points, eyed needles), and so do the earliest European [painted caves](event:cave-art).

name: Peopling of the Americas
summary: Humans crossed Beringia and dispersed southward along the Pacific coast, colonizing two empty continents.
body:
Part of [Out of Africa dispersal](event:out-of-africa). The Americas were the last continents people reached. The academic consensus places arrival between about 20,000 and 15,000 years ago, by way of Beringia, the land bridge exposed between Siberia and Alaska while sea level was low.

Genetic work describes the sequence. An Ancient Beringian population separated from Siberians around 36,000 years ago, was effectively isolated by about 25,000, and split into the lineages ancestral to later Native American populations between 17,000 and 14,500 years ago.

The route south was long assumed to be the ice-free corridor between the Laurentide and Cordilleran ice sheets, but that corridor became biologically passable only around 13,000 to 12,000 years ago, which is too late for the earliest sites. A Pacific coastal route, supported by kelp forests and marine resources, is now the more common explanation.

Monte Verde in southern Chile, at 14,500 years, was the first site widely accepted as older than the Clovis culture, and others followed: Buttermilk Creek in Texas at 15,500, Paisley Caves in Oregon at 14,300, Swan Point in Alaska at 14,000. Human footprints at White Sands in New Mexico have been dated to as much as 23,000 years ago; that dating has been challenged and re-defended and is not settled. However it began, the spread was fast, and people reached the southern end of South America within a few thousand years of entering the continent.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settlement_of_the_Americas).

name: Start of the Holocene
summary: The current interglacial commenced, establishing the stable, warm climate in which all human civilisation developed.
body:
The Holocene is the current geological epoch, beginning 11,700 years before 2000 and continuing to the present. It is the interglacial that followed the last glaciation, and every settled human society has existed within it.

Its base is defined not by a date but by a physical section: a horizon in the NGRIP2 ice core from central Greenland marking the end of the [Younger Dryas](event:younger-dryas), ratified as the epoch's global stratotype in 2008. The warming it records was several degrees within a few decades.

Three ages were formally defined in 2018. The Greenlandian runs from 11,700 to 8,200 years ago; the Northgrippian from 8,200 to 4,200, beginning at the 8.2-kiloyear cold event caused by the final drainage of the North American proglacial lakes; and the Meghalayan from 4,200 years ago to the present, beginning with a drought of roughly two centuries recorded across the northern hemisphere.

Sea level rose tens of metres over the first few thousand years as the ice sheets melted, then stabilised. The climate has been comparatively steady, though not without variability, including the 8.2-kiloyear event and cycles of between one and two and a half thousand years. [Agriculture](event:agriculture) was adopted independently in several regions between about 10,000 and 7,000 years ago.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocene).

name: Dawn of agriculture
summary: Farming was developed independently in several regions, beginning with the Fertile Crescent, and permanently changed how humans live.
body:
Agriculture is the deliberate cultivation of plants and herding of animals. It was taken up independently in at least eleven regions of the world between roughly 10,000 and 4,000 BCE, the earliest and best documented beginning being in the Fertile Crescent, the arc of hill country running from the Levant through southern Anatolia to the Zagros. The shift from foraging to farming is usually called the Neolithic Revolution, although it took thousands of years.

Eight founder crops were domesticated in the Fertile Crescent: emmer and einkorn wheat, barley, lentil, pea, chickpea, bitter vetch and flax. Sheep, goats, pigs and cattle followed. Elsewhere the same shift began from different material: rice and millet in China, maize, beans and squash in Mesoamerica, potatoes and quinoa in the Andes, sorghum and yams in Africa, taro and banana in New Guinea.

Farming produced storable surpluses, and surpluses supported permanent villages, property, craft specialisation, hierarchy, and eventually cities and states. It also fed far more people from the same ground: world population, small and slow-growing throughout the Palaeolithic, began a rise that has not stopped.

The costs are visible in the skeletons. Early farmers were shorter than the foragers before them, had worse teeth and more signs of nutritional stress, and worked longer hours on a narrower diet. Living beside dense herds also gave humans measles, smallpox, influenza and tuberculosis.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic_Revolution).

steps.name: The founder crops of the Fertile Crescent
steps.page: Wild stands of emmer and einkorn wheat, barley and pulses were harvested in the Levant and upper Mesopotamia long before they were sown. Over roughly a millennium the harvested populations changed: seed heads stopped shattering, grains grew larger, and the plants became dependent on people to sow them. This is the domestication of the eight founder crops, the best documented of the early origins of farming.

steps.name: Rice farming in the Yangtze valley
steps.page: Rice was domesticated from wild stands in the middle and lower Yangtze; millet was domesticated separately on the drier loess soils of the Yellow River basin. The two are the agricultural foundation of Chinese civilisation, and both were domesticated independently of the Fertile Crescent.

steps.name: Maize domesticated in Mexico
steps.page: Maize was bred out of teosinte, a grass whose ear is a fraction of the size, in the Balsas river valley of southern Mexico. Combined later with beans and squash, it became the staple of every Mesoamerican and, eventually, of much of North America and the Andes.

steps.name: Farming reaches Europe
steps.page: Farmers moved from Anatolia into Greece and the Balkans, then up the Danube and along the Mediterranean coast, carrying the Fertile Crescent crop package with them. Ancient DNA shows this was largely a migration of people rather than the spread of an idea: European farmers descend substantially from Anatolian ancestors, mixed to varying degrees with the hunter-gatherers already there.

name: Invention of writing
summary: Cuneiform accounting marks in Sumer became the first true writing system, with Egyptian hieroglyphs following within a century or two.
body:
Writing is the recording of language in visible signs. It was invented independently at least three and probably four times: in Sumer around 3200 BCE, in Egypt at almost the same date, in China by about 1200 BCE, and in Mesoamerica by about 500 BCE. The Sumerian system is the earliest for which the development can be followed step by step.

It began as accounting. Clay tokens representing quantities of grain, oil and livestock were sealed in clay envelopes, then impressed on the outside of them, then drawn on flat tablets as pictographs, a running record of what the temples of [Uruk](event:uruk) had received and paid out. Signs were pressed into damp clay with a reed stylus, which turned curved pictures into wedge-shaped strokes: cuneiform. The decisive move was phonetic. Once a sign could stand for the sound of a word rather than the thing, names, verbs and grammar could be written, and the system could record anything the language could say.

Egyptian hieroglyphs appear within a century or two, complete enough that borrowing of the idea is likely even though the signs are unrelated. Chinese writing is first attested on Shang [oracle bones](event:oracle-bones); Maya and Zapotec scripts arose with no contact with the Old World at all. All of them came to be used for law, contracts, literature and mathematics, and they leave records that historians can read directly rather than infer.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_writing).

name: Unification of Egypt
summary: Upper and Lower Egypt were unified under a single king, traditionally Narmer, beginning three millennia of pharaonic civilisation.
body:
Around 3100 BCE Upper and Lower Egypt (the Nile valley and the Delta) were brought under a single king, beginning the Early Dynastic Period and roughly three thousand years of pharaonic rule. Tradition names the first king Menes; he is usually identified with Narmer, and possibly with his successor Hor-Aha.

The unification is attested less by a narrative than by objects. The Narmer Palette, a ceremonial siltstone plaque from Hierakonpolis, shows the king wearing the white crown of Upper Egypt on one face and the red crown of Lower Egypt on the other, striking down a captive. Whether it records a single conquest or commemorates a process already long under way is disputed; the material culture of Upper Egypt had been spreading north for generations.

What emerged was a centralised state: a divine kingship, a capital at Memphis at the junction of the two lands, a system of nomes administered by royal officials, a national grain tax based on the Nile flood, and hieroglyphic writing to record it. Royal tombs at Abydos and later the pyramid field at Saqqara mark its wealth. The state survived three later periods of collapse and reunification.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Dynastic_Period_(Egypt)).

name: Great Pyramid of Giza
summary: Khufu's tomb, 146 metres tall and built from over two million blocks, was the tallest structure on Earth for 3,800 years.
body:
Part of [Unification of Egypt](event:egypt-unification). The Great Pyramid of Giza was built as the tomb of the Fourth Dynasty pharaoh Khufu, around 2560 BCE, over an estimated twenty years. At 146.6 m it was the tallest structure made by human beings for some 3,800 years, and it is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing.

It contains roughly 2.3 million blocks of limestone and granite, most of them quarried on the plateau itself, with the fine casing limestone brought from Tura across the river and the granite of the burial chamber from Aswan, 800 km upstream. The base is level to within a few centimetres and the sides are aligned on the cardinal directions to a fraction of a degree. Inside are three chambers, a corbelled Grand Gallery and a set of narrow shafts whose function is still argued.

The workers' town excavated south-east of the pyramid, with bakeries, breweries and cattle bones, together with papyri from Wadi al-Jarf recording a gang delivering casing stone, indicate a paid and organised workforce housed and fed by the state rather than the mass of slaves of later legend. How the blocks were raised is not recorded; ramps of several geometries have been proposed and none is proven. The casing was stripped in the medieval period, leaving the stepped core visible today.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza).

name: Life of the Buddha
summary: Siddhartha Gautama taught in the Ganges plain, founding one of the world's great religious and philosophical traditions.
body:
Siddhartha Gautama, later called the Buddha ('the awakened one'), was a teacher who lived in the eastern Ganges plain and founded the community and the body of teaching that became Buddhism. Tradition places his life in 563–483 BCE; much modern scholarship dates his death a century later, between about 480 and 400 BCE.

He was born into the Shakya clan at Lumbini, in what is now Nepal, the son of a local ruler. The traditional life has him leaving his family and household at twenty-nine, studying under teachers of meditation and then practising severe asceticism for six years, and abandoning both extremes for what he called the middle way. He reached awakening in meditation under a tree at Bodh Gaya, and gave his first discourse in the deer park at Sarnath near Varanasi.

His teaching is summarised in the Four Noble Truths: that existence involves suffering, that suffering arises from craving, that it can cease, and that a path leads to its cessation, the Noble Eightfold Path of right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration. He taught that nothing has a permanent self and that all things arise in dependence on conditions. He accepted no caste distinction among his followers.

He taught for some forty-five years across Magadha and Kosala, and organised a monastic community, the sangha, which outlived him. He died at Kushinagar, aged about eighty. His words were preserved by recitation and not written down for several centuries, first in the Pali Canon. Under [Ashoka](event:maurya-empire) the religion spread beyond India, and it later travelled the [Silk Road](event:spread-buddhism) into Central Asia and China.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gautama_Buddha).

name: Confucius
summary: Kong Qiu taught an ethic of duty, ritual propriety and learning that shaped Chinese government and society for two millennia.
body:
Part of [Zhou Dynasty](event:zhou-dynasty). Confucius (Kong Qiu, honorifically Kongzi, 'Master Kong') was a Chinese teacher and official who lived from 551 to 479 BCE, in the Spring and Autumn period of the [Zhou](event:zhou-dynasty), when the royal house had lost authority and the states fought among themselves. He taught that order is restored by cultivating character, not by force, and his ideas became the working philosophy of the Chinese state.

He was born in the small state of Lu, in modern Shandong, held minor office there, and spent much of his later life travelling from court to court in search of a ruler who would apply his ideas. None did. He is said to have taught some three thousand students, and to have taken pupils regardless of their birth.

His central terms are *ren*, humaneness or fellow feeling; *li*, the ritual propriety that governs how people treat one another; *xiao*, devotion to parents; and the *junzi*, the exemplary person, a title he redefined from noble birth to moral quality. Government, he held, works by the example the ruler sets: correct names, correct conduct, and the people follow. He described himself as a transmitter rather than an innovator, appealing to the practice of the early Zhou.

The *Analects*, a collection of his sayings and conversations, was compiled by later followers. Mencius and Xunzi developed the tradition in opposite directions; the Qin suppressed it; the [Han](event:han-dynasty) made it official, and from the seventh century CE the Confucian classics were the syllabus of the imperial examinations that selected officials until 1905.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confucius).

name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
summary: Cyrus the Great and his successors ruled from the Aegean to the Indus, the largest empire the world had seen.
body:
The Achaemenid Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great about 550 BCE, was the first Persian empire and the largest state the world had yet seen. At its height it ran from the Aegean and Egypt to the Indus, and it was governed as a single administrative system rather than as a collection of tributaries.

Cyrus overthrew his Median overlord, took Lydia and the Greek cities of Ionia in 547 BCE, and entered Babylon in 539. The Cyrus Cylinder records his restoration of local cults; the Hebrew Bible remembers him for allowing the Judean exiles to return and rebuild the temple. His son Cambyses II added Egypt in 525. Darius I, who seized the throne in 522 and justified it in the trilingual Behistun inscription, reorganised the empire into some twenty satrapies, each under a governor watched by royal inspectors, with fixed tribute in silver, a standard gold coin (the daric), an imperial post and the Royal Road running some 2,700 km from Sardis to Susa. Aramaic served as the language of administration. Persepolis was begun as a ceremonial capital, alongside Susa, Ecbatana and Babylon.

The empire held perhaps forty million people, a large share of the world's population at the time, and generally let subject peoples keep their languages, laws and religions. Its western expansion failed against the Greek city-states in the [Greco-Persian Wars](event:greco-persian-wars). It fell in four years to [Alexander](event:alexander-conquests): Gaugamela in 331 BCE, Persepolis burned the following year, and Darius III killed by his own satrap in 330.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire).

name: Athenian democracy
summary: The reforms of Cleisthenes gave political power to the assembly of citizens, inventing direct democracy.
body:
Athenian democracy was the system under which the citizens of Athens governed themselves directly, from the reforms of Cleisthenes in 508/507 BCE until the city lost its independence in 322 BCE. It is the first political system known to have been called a democracy, and the first for which the workings are documented in detail.

Cleisthenes broke the hold of the aristocratic clans by reorganising the citizen body into ten new tribes, each drawn from villages in three separate parts of Attica so that no tribe was a regional faction. A Council of 500, fifty from each tribe and chosen by lot for a year, prepared business; the Assembly, open to every adult male citizen, met about forty times a year on the Pnyx to decide it. Ephialtes stripped the old aristocratic council of the Areopagus of its political powers in 462 BCE, and under Pericles the state paid jurors, and later assembly-goers, so that poorer citizens could attend.

Selection by lot rather than election was central: it treated any citizen as competent to judge, and only the generalships and a few technical offices were filled by vote. Ostracism allowed the Assembly to exile a citizen for ten years without charge.

The citizen body numbered perhaps 30,000 adult men out of a population of some 250,000. Women, resident foreigners and a large enslaved population had no vote. The system was overthrown twice during the [Peloponnesian War](event:peloponnesian-war) and restored both times; it ended after the Lamian War, when Macedon imposed a property qualification. The idea it began is treated in [democracy](item:democracy).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athenian_democracy).

name: Democracy
summary: Rule by the people: the principle that political authority derives from those subject to it, and the institutions built to make that workable.
body:
The word is Greek, and so is the first documented example. The reforms of Cleisthenes in 508 BCE reorganised [Athens](item:athenian-democracy) so that policy was decided by an assembly of citizens and offices were filled largely by lot. It was direct, not representative, and the citizen body excluded women, resident foreigners and a very large enslaved population, and perhaps a seventh of the adults present had a vote.

The Athenian institution did not survive antiquity, but its vocabulary did. Roman republicanism, the limits placed on a king by [Magna Carta](item:magna-carta), and the Dutch and English revolutions supplied the vocabulary of consent, representation and the rule of law; the [American](item:us-constitution) and [French](item:rights-of-man) revolutions turned it into written constitutions asserting rights against the state.

The franchise widened slowly and unevenly: property qualifications, then [women's suffrage](item:finland-suffrage) from 1906, then the [American civil rights](item:civil-rights-act) legislation of the 1960s and the [end of apartheid](item:apartheid-end) in 1994. The count of electoral democracies rose through the twentieth century and has fallen back since about 2010.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy).

name: Conquests of Alexander the Great
summary: In eleven years Alexander of Macedon destroyed the Persian Empire and led an army from Greece to the Punjab.
body:
Alexander III of Macedon crossed into Asia in 334 BCE and by 330 had destroyed the [Achaemenid Empire](event:achaemenid-empire), the largest state of its day. He campaigned for another seven years, as far as the Punjab, and died at Babylon in 323 BCE at the age of thirty-two, having never lost a battle.

He inherited the plan and the army from his father Philip II, who had made Macedon the dominant power in Greece and drilled an infantry armed with the long *sarissa* pike, supported by heavy Companion cavalry. Alexander's method was consistent: pin the enemy line with the phalanx, find or force a gap, and drive the cavalry through it at the enemy commander. Three victories (the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela) broke Persian field armies, and sieges of Tyre and Gaza showed that fortified cities would not hold him either.

He was crowned in Egypt, burned the palace at Persepolis, took the Persian royal title and much of the Persian administration with it, married the Bactrian Roxana, ordered mass marriages between his officers and Iranian women, and kept satraps in place, policies that his Macedonians resented. His army finally refused to go further east at the Hyphasis.

He left no viable heir. Within a generation his generals had divided the conquests into the Seleucid, Ptolemaic and Antigonid kingdoms. The Greek language, coinage, city plan and civic institutions they carried with them reached from [Egypt](event:alexandria) to Afghanistan.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_Alexander_the_Great).

steps.name: Crossing into Asia: the Granicus
steps.page: Alexander crossed the Hellespont in the spring of 334 BCE with about 40,000 men and met the satraps' army at the river Granicus in May. He attacked across the river at once. The victory opened western Anatolia; he took the Ionian cities and, at Gordium, is said to have cut the knot that was supposed to be untied only by the future ruler of Asia.

steps.name: Issus
steps.page: Darius III brought the royal army round behind Alexander and cut his supply line, forcing a battle on a narrow coastal plain in Cilicia in November 333 BCE where his numbers could not be used. The Persian line broke, Darius fled the field, and his mother, wife and daughters were captured in the camp.

steps.name: The siege of Tyre
steps.page: Rather than pursue Darius, Alexander turned south to take the Phoenician ports and deny the Persian fleet its bases. Tyre, on an island half a kilometre offshore, held out for seven months in 332 BCE until a mole was built out to its walls. Gaza fell after two months more, and Egypt surrendered without a fight.

steps.name: Persepolis and the death of Darius
steps.page: Babylon and Susa surrendered with their treasuries. Alexander forced the Persian Gates in winter and entered Persepolis, whose palace was burned in 330 BCE. Whether that was policy or the result of a drinking party was already argued in antiquity. Darius, a fugitive, was killed by his own satrap Bessus that summer, and Alexander had him buried as a king and took the title himself.

steps.name: Bactria and Sogdiana
steps.page: The eastern satrapies took three years and cost more than the Persian field armies had. Alexander fought a war of forts, raids and reprisals across what is now Afghanistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, founded garrison cities, took the Sogdian Rock, and married Roxana. It was in these years that he killed his officer Cleitus in a quarrel and that a conspiracy among his pages was uncovered.

steps.name: The Hydaspes and the Hyphasis
steps.page: Crossing into the Punjab in 326 BCE, Alexander beat King Porus at the Hydaspes in a monsoon river crossing, his hardest-fought battle and the first against war elephants in numbers. At the next river, the Hyphasis, the army refused to go on. He turned south down the Indus instead of east.

steps.name: The return through Gedrosia
steps.page: From the Indus delta the fleet under Nearchus followed the coast while Alexander marched the army back through the Gedrosian desert in what is now Baluchistan, in the autumn and winter of 325 BCE. Thirst, heat and a flash flood killed a large part of the column and most of the followers with it, the worst losses of the whole expedition and the only ones not inflicted by an enemy.

steps.name: Death at Babylon
steps.page: Alexander returned to Babylon and was planning an expedition into Arabia when he fell ill after a long banquet and died eleven days later, in June 323 BCE, aged thirty-two. Fever, poison and heavy drinking have all been proposed. Asked who should succeed him, he is reported to have said 'the strongest'; his generals fought over the answer for forty years.

name: Qin unification of China
summary: Ying Zheng conquered the six rival states, declared himself First Emperor, and imposed one script, one currency and one law on China.
body:
Between 230 and 221 BCE the state of Qin conquered the six kingdoms that had divided China since the [Zhou](event:zhou-dynasty) court lost control of them, and its king Ying Zheng took the new title Shi Huangdi, First Emperor. The dynasty he founded lasted fifteen years; the unified empire it created has been restored again and again ever since.

Qin's advantage was a century of Legalist reform. Beginning with Shang Yang in the fourth century BCE, it had replaced hereditary privilege with promotion by military merit, registered its population in mutually liable households, taxed land directly and codified harsh, uniformly applied law. It could therefore raise, feed and move armies its neighbours could not match.

After the conquest, the aristocracies of the defeated states were moved to the capital and their walls pulled down. The empire was divided into commanderies and counties run by appointed officials rather than by hereditary lords, the framework of Chinese administration for the next two thousand years. Weights, measures, coinage, the width of cart axles and the writing system were standardised, and the small seal script imposed on all of them.

The same methods drew lasting criticism. Books held to encourage criticism of the present by appeal to the past were ordered burned, scholars were executed, and hundreds of thousands were conscripted for the [Great Wall](event:great-wall), the road network and the emperor's [tomb](event:terracotta-army). The First Emperor died in 210 BCE while touring the east, and rebellion brought the dynasty down within four years, leaving the [Han](event:han-dynasty) to inherit the machinery he had built.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_dynasty).

steps.name: The conquest of the six states
steps.page: Qin took Han in 230 BCE, Zhao in 228, Wei in 225, Chu (the largest and hardest, needing an army said to be 600,000 strong) in 223, Yan in 222 and Qi, which surrendered without a fight, in 221. Nine years ended more than five centuries of warfare between the Chinese states.

steps.name: Ying Zheng becomes the First Emperor
steps.page: In 221 BCE Ying Zheng judged the old title of king inadequate and coined a new one, huangdi, joining the words for the mythical sovereigns and thearchs: Shi Huangdi, First Emperor, with his successors to be numbered after him. The empire was divided into thirty-six commanderies under appointed governors, and the capital fixed at Xianyang.

steps.name: One script, one coin, one axle
steps.page: The chancellor Li Si oversaw the standardisation of the writing system on a simplified seal script, of weights and measures, and of currency on a round bronze coin with a square hole that outlasted every dynasty that issued it. Cart axles were fixed to a single width so that wheels would run in the ruts of the new imperial roads, and the noble families of the conquered states were resettled at the capital.

steps.name: The burning of the books
steps.page: On Li Si's proposal in 213 BCE, private copies of the classics, of poetry and of the histories of the conquered states were ordered surrendered and burned; manuals of medicine, divination and agriculture were exempt, and copies were kept in the imperial archive. Tradition adds the burial alive of scholars the following year. Later Confucian historians treated the episode as the defining crime of the dynasty, and modern scholars regard their account as coloured by it.

steps.name: Rebellion and the fall of Qin
steps.page: The First Emperor died on tour in 210 BCE; his death was concealed until the succession could be fixed on a compliant younger son. Within a year conscripts who would have been executed for arriving late rose in revolt, and the old aristocracies rose with them. Xianyang fell in 206 BCE. Liu Bang, a village official turned rebel, beat his rival Xiang Yu and founded the [Han](event:han-dynasty) in 202.

name: Silk Road trade network
summary: Caravan routes linked China, Central Asia, Persia, India and the Mediterranean for some fifteen centuries.
body:
The Silk Road is the name given to the network of overland routes that linked China with Central Asia, Persia, India and the Mediterranean from about the second century BCE to the fifteenth century CE. Goods, people, ideas and disease moved along it, usually in relays rather than end to end.

The conventional starting point is the mission of Zhang Qian, sent west by the [Han](event:han-dynasty) court in 138 BCE to seek allies against the Xiongnu. He was held captive for years and came back with the first Chinese account of the states of Central Asia, and regular traffic followed. The routes ran from Chang'an through the Gansu corridor, split around the Taklamakan desert at its string of oasis towns (Dunhuang, Kashgar, Samarkand), and continued to Persia, the Levantine ports and, by sea, to India.

Very few merchants travelled the whole distance. Sogdian and later Arab and Persian traders worked stages of it, and a bolt of silk might change hands many times between China and Antioch. Silk went west, along with lacquer and later porcelain; horses, glass, wool, silver and gold came east. Ideas travelled as well: [Buddhism](event:spread-buddhism) travelled into China this way, [paper](event:paper-invention) travelled out, and Nestorian Christianity, Manichaeism and Islam all followed the same channels.

Traffic was safest under strong empires and worst in the gaps between them; the Mongol peace of the thirteenth century was its last great period. The [Black Death](event:black-death) almost certainly reached Europe along these routes. The wider network is treated in [the Silk Roads](item:silk-roads).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road).

name: The Silk Roads
summary: The overland and maritime routes that connected China, India, Persia and the Mediterranean, and the exchange of goods, technologies, religions and disease along them.
body:
The name is a nineteenth-century coinage for something that was never a single road. [The routes](item:silk-road) were a shifting web of caravan stages and sea lanes, worked in relays by merchants who rarely travelled their whole length; a bolt of silk might change hands twenty times between Chang'an and Antioch.

Goods moved in both directions (silk, porcelain and rhubarb west; horses, glass, silver and cotton east), and ideas moved with them. [Paper](item:paper-invention) reached Samarkand and then the Islamic world and Europe; [Buddhism](item:spread-buddhism) travelled from India into Central Asia and China; gunpowder, the compass and Indian numerals followed the same channels. The [Han](item:han-dynasty) mission of Zhang Qian in 130 BCE is the conventional starting point, and the *Pax Mongolica* under [Genghis Khan's](item:temujin-genghis-khan) successors its safest period, when [Marco Polo](item:marco-polo) made the journey.

Disease used the roads too: the [Black Death](item:black-death) almost certainly reached Europe along them. The overland trade declined as the Ming turned inward after [Zheng He](item:zheng-he-admiral) and as Portuguese ships opened a sea route to the Indies, but the maritime leg never stopped.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road).

name: Founding of the Roman Empire
summary: The Senate granted Octavian the name Augustus and effective sole power, beginning two centuries of Roman peace.
body:
In January 27 BCE the Senate granted Octavian, sole victor of the civil wars, the name Augustus and a command over the provinces where most of the legions were stationed. The arrangement is conventionally taken as the founding of the Roman Empire, and it began two centuries of relative internal peace.

Augustus was careful never to hold a title that sounded like monarchy. He was *princeps*, first citizen; the Senate met, magistrates were elected, and the forms of the [Republic](event:roman-republic-fall) continued. What he actually held was control of the army, of the treasury of the provinces that paid for it, and of the succession. The system is called the principate.

The empire he left ran from Spain to Syria and from Britain (added in 43 CE) to the Sahara, holding perhaps fifty to sixty million people, a fifth or more of the world's population. It was governed with a small administration: local elites collected the taxes and ran the towns, and Roman citizenship, extended steadily and finally to nearly all free inhabitants in 212 CE, was the reward for cooperation. One currency, one body of [law](event:roman-law-growth), a professional standing army of some thirty legions and a network of [roads](event:roman-roads) held it together.

The *Pax Romana* ran to the [death of Marcus Aurelius](event:marcus-aurelius) in 180 CE. The empire survived crisis, division and [Christianisation](event:constantine), and its western half [ended in 476](event:rome-fall); the eastern continued from [Constantinople](event:constantinople-founded) for another thousand years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire).

name: Crucifixion of Jesus
summary: Jesus of Nazareth was executed in Roman Judaea; his followers' claim that he rose again founded Christianity.
body:
Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish preacher from Galilee, was executed by crucifixion in Jerusalem under the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate, most probably in 30 or 33 CE. His followers' claim that he had risen from the dead is the origin of Christianity.

Crucifixion was a Roman penalty for slaves, rebels and provincials, designed to be slow and public. The gospels describe an arrest after a meal at Passover, a hearing before the Jewish authorities, a trial before Pilate on a charge that amounted to sedition, and execution outside the city walls between two others, with a placard naming him King of the Jews. That he was crucified under Pilate is one of the few points about him attested outside Christian writing: the Roman historian Tacitus mentions it, as does Josephus.

The movement that followed was at first one of several Jewish groups. Its decisive turn came with Paul of Tarsus, who preached to non-Jews and dropped the requirement of circumcision and the food laws, making the message portable across the Roman world. Written gospels followed in the decades after 70 CE.

Within three centuries the religion had [spread across the empire](event:spread-christianity) that executed him, and after [Constantine](event:constantine) it became the religion of the Roman state. Christianity is today the largest religion in the world, with over two billion adherents, and the Western calendar still counts its years from a sixth-century estimate of his birth.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crucifixion_of_Jesus).

name: Constantine legalises Christianity
summary: The Edict of Milan ended the persecution of Christians and set the empire on the path to a Christian state.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). In 313 CE the emperors Constantine and Licinius agreed at Milan to end the persecution of Christians, grant freedom of worship to everyone in the empire, and return confiscated church property. The agreement, usually called the Edict of Milan, is the point at which Christianity became a legal religion of the Roman state.

It followed the worst persecution the church had faced, begun by Diocletian in 303, and Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome in 312, which he attributed to the Christian God after a vision reported in different forms by different writers.

Constantine went much further than toleration. He exempted clergy from public duties, funded church building at Rome and Jerusalem, gave bishops civil jurisdiction, and intervened directly in doctrinal disputes, summoning and presiding over the [Council of Nicaea](event:nicaea) in 325 to settle the question of Christ's relation to the Father. He [founded a new capital](event:constantinople-founded) at Byzantium, laid out with churches rather than temples. He was baptised only on his deathbed in 337, which was not unusual at the time.

Traditional cults were not banned and remained legal for most of the century. In 380 the Edict of Thessalonica made Nicene Christianity the official religion of the empire, and by the end of the century sacrifice had been prohibited. The church acquired wealth, hierarchy and imperial protection in the space of two generations.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Milan).

name: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
summary: The last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed at Ravenna, ending Roman rule in the west.
body:
In 476 CE the commander Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, the last emperor to rule in Italy, and did not replace him. The date is conventionally given as the end of the Western Roman Empire, though nothing much happened on it and contemporaries did not treat it as an ending.

The decline was long and had many causes, and historians have never agreed on their weight. Recurring civil wars and short reigns; the loss of Africa, Spain and Gaul to the peoples of the [migration period](event:migration-period), and with them the tax revenue that paid the army; a currency debased and an administration that could no longer collect; armies increasingly recruited from outside the empire and commanded by men whose loyalty was personal; plague and a colder, drier climate. The [sack of Rome in 410](event:rome-sack-410) and again in 455 showed how little was left to defend it.

By the 470s the western emperor governed little beyond Italy, and real power lay with his generals. Odoacer sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and asked to rule Italy as a patrician under the eastern emperor. The legal fiction of a single empire continued.

The western provinces became the Germanic successor kingdoms, in which Roman law, Latin and the church survived while the tax state and the standing army did not.
