The eastern half, ruled from [Constantinople](event:constantinople-founded), was not affected and lasted until 1453. 'The fall of Rome' is therefore a statement about the west, and about a process rather than a year.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire).

name: The Hijra and the founding of Islam
summary: Muhammad and his followers migrated from Mecca to Medina, founding the first Muslim community; the year is year one of the Islamic calendar.
body:
In 622 Muhammad and his followers left Mecca for the oasis town of Yathrib, afterwards called Medina, following years of hostility from the Meccan leadership. The migration, the *hijra*, is the event from which the Islamic calendar counts its years. At Medina the community became a political body as well as a religious one, with Muhammad as its leader and arbitrator.

Muhammad had begun preaching in Mecca around 610, teaching the oneness of God, the duty of charity and a coming judgement, in a city whose trade and standing rested partly on pilgrimage to its shrines. His followers were a small and increasingly harassed minority, and some had already taken refuge in Christian Ethiopia. An invitation from clans at Yathrib, who wanted an outside arbitrator for their own long feud, gave the community somewhere to go.

The Medinan decade produced practices central to Islam since: communal prayer, the fast of Ramadan, the alms tax and the direction of prayer turned toward Mecca. It also produced a running conflict with the Meccans that ended with the surrender of Mecca in 630. By Muhammad's death in 632 most of the Arabian peninsula had accepted his authority.

The revelations he recited were collected as the Quran within a generation. His successors, the caliphs, disagreed over who had the right to lead, a dispute that separated Sunni and Shia Islam. Within a century their armies ruled from Spain to the Indus (see the [early Muslim conquests](event:islamic-conquests)). Islam is today the second largest religion in the world, with about 1.9 billion adherents.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijrah).

name: Early Muslim conquests
summary: Arab armies took Persia, the Levant, Egypt, North Africa and most of Spain within roughly a century of Muhammad's death.
body:
Part of [The Hijra and the founding of Islam](event:hijra). In the century after Muhammad's death in 632, armies from Arabia destroyed the Sasanian empire outright and took the southern and eastern provinces of Byzantium, then North Africa and most of the Iberian peninsula. It was one of the fastest territorial expansions in recorded history: from the Arabian peninsula to an empire reaching from the Atlantic to the Indus.

Both of the powers the Arabs faced had just fought each other to exhaustion in a war lasting from 602 to 628, and neither could replace a lost field army quickly. The Arab forces were mobile, unified under the authority of the caliphs at Medina and later the Umayyads at Damascus, and willing to campaign far from home. Persia was conquered entirely; Byzantium survived behind the Taurus mountains but lost Syria, Palestine, Egypt and North Africa, and never recovered them.

Conquest was not conversion. Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians who submitted kept their religion and paid a poll tax, and for the first century Muslims were a ruling minority living largely in new garrison towns such as Basra, Kufa and Fustat. Conversion of the conquered populations happened slowly, over several centuries.

The advance stopped at recognisable limits: the Anatolian plateau and the walls of Constantinople in the north, the Pyrenees and the Franks at [Tours](event:tours) in the west, the mountains and deserts of the Indian and Central Asian frontiers in the east. The Umayyad caliphate that had assembled it was overthrown by the Abbasids in 750, and the empire began to divide into separate states.

The campaigns ran in distinct phases, listed as steps.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Muslim_conquests).

steps.name: The Ridda wars
steps.page: Muhammad's death in 632 left it unclear whether the tribes of Arabia had submitted to him personally or to the community he led. Several repudiated Medina's authority, and some followed rival prophets. The first caliph, Abu Bakr, spent a year forcing them back by arms. The wars ended with Arabia unified under Medina and with an army in the field that had nowhere left to fight.

steps.name: Into Syria and Iraq
steps.page: Columns sent north from Medina raided the Byzantine border provinces and the Sasanian lands of lower Iraq at the same time. Damascus fell in 634. Khalid ibn al-Walid marched a force across the desert from Iraq to Syria to join the western campaign, a move the sources treat as the decisive stroke of the war.

steps.name: The fall of Sasanian Persia
steps.page: The victory at al-Qadisiyyah in 636 opened Mesopotamia and the Sasanian capital of Ctesiphon. The Persian army was broken again at Nahavand in 642, after which the empire was taken province by province. The last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, was killed in flight near Merv in 651. Unlike Byzantium, the Sasanian state did not survive at all.

steps.name: Egypt and Alexandria
steps.page: Amr ibn al-As entered Egypt in 639 with a small force, took the fortress of Babylon on the Nile in 641 and accepted the surrender of Alexandria in 642. He founded a garrison town, Fustat, beside the fortress; Cairo later grew from it. Egypt's grain, which had fed Constantinople, now fed the caliphate.

steps.name: Across North Africa
steps.page: The advance west was slower, fought against Byzantine garrisons and against Berber confederations who resisted for decades. Qayrawan was founded as a base in 670, Carthage taken in 698, and the Atlantic coast reached by about 709. Berber converts made up much of the army that crossed into Spain.

steps.name: Al-Andalus
steps.page: Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed the strait in 711 with a mainly Berber force and destroyed the Visigothic king Roderic's army. The kingdom collapsed quickly and most of the peninsula was under Muslim rule by 718. Christian resistance survived in the northern mountains, which is where the [Reconquista](event:reconquista) begins.

name: The Crusades
summary: Two centuries of religious warfare launched from Latin Europe against the Muslim states of the eastern Mediterranean.
body:
The Crusades were a series of wars called by the papacy, fought mainly between 1095 and 1291, in which armies from Latin Europe attacked Muslim states in the eastern Mediterranean and held territory there. Those who took the cross were promised remission of the penalties of sin. Four Crusader states were established in the Levant after the first expedition; the last of them was lost in 1291.

The immediate occasion was a Byzantine appeal for troops after [Manzikert](event:manzikert). Behind it lay a papacy asserting leadership over Latin Christendom, a warrior aristocracy with more sons than land, and an established practice of armed pilgrimage. Pope Urban II preached the first expedition at Clermont in 1095; the response was far larger than he had asked for.

Only the first campaign achieved its stated aim. Later expeditions were beaten, diverted or negotiated away, and the [Fourth](event:fourth-crusade) sacked Christian Constantinople instead. Crusades were also preached elsewhere: against the Muslims of [Iberia](event:reconquista), against pagans on the Baltic, and against heretics in southern France. The model outlasted the Levantine wars by centuries.

The consequences were mixed and are still argued over. Trade with the Levant grew and Italian ports profited; Arabic science and Greek texts came west through Spain and Sicily more than through Syria; Jewish communities in the Rhineland were massacred by armies on their way east; and the sack of Constantinople left Byzantium permanently weakened. In the Muslim world the wars were a frontier problem rather than a defining event, and were given their modern symbolic weight only in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

The numbered expeditions are listed as steps.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusades).

steps.name: Urban II preaches at Clermont
steps.page: At the council of Clermont on 27 November 1095, Pope Urban II called on the knighthood of France to march east, to help the eastern Christians and to recover Jerusalem, and offered remission of penance to those who went. Preachers carried the appeal far beyond the intended audience, and poorly organised popular bands set out ahead of the armies, attacking Jewish communities in the Rhineland on the way; most were destroyed in Anatolia.

steps.name: The Crusader states
steps.page: Four Latin states were left behind by the first expedition: the kingdom of Jerusalem, the county of Tripoli, the principality of Antioch and the county of Edessa. They were small, dependent on a stream of pilgrims and reinforcements, and held together by castles and by the [military orders](event:knights-templar). Their neighbours were divided, which is much of why they survived at all.

steps.name: Second Crusade
steps.page: The loss of Edessa in 1144 brought a second expedition, preached by Bernard of Clairvaux and led by the kings of France and Germany. Both armies were badly mauled crossing Anatolia, and the attack they made on Damascus, a city then friendly to Jerusalem, collapsed after four days. The failure damaged the standing of crusading in Europe for a generation.

steps.name: Third Crusade
steps.page: The emperor Frederick Barbarossa, Philip II of France and Richard I of England went east in response. Frederick drowned on the way, Philip went home after the fall of Acre, and Richard beat Saladin at Arsuf and twice came within reach of Jerusalem without attacking it. The truce of 1192 left the Latins a coastal strip and pilgrims the right of access to the city.

steps.name: The Egyptian crusades
steps.page: Later strategy aimed at Egypt, the base of Ayyubid power. The Fifth Crusade took Damietta in 1219 and lost it in 1221 when the Nile flooded around its army. Frederick II recovered Jerusalem by treaty in 1229 without fighting, and the city was lost again in 1244. Louis IX of France repeated the Damietta plan in 1249, was defeated at Mansurah and captured, and was ransomed in 1250.

name: Genghis Khan
summary: Mongol ruler who united the steppe tribes and founded the largest contiguous land empire in history.
body:
Born Temüjin, the son of a minor chieftain poisoned when the boy was nine, he grew up in poverty and captivity on the eastern steppe. Through alliance, patronage and a series of steppe wars he united the Mongol and Turkic tribes, and in 1206 an assembly [proclaimed him Genghis Khan](item:genghis-khan), universal ruler.

He reorganised his followers into decimal units that cut across tribal loyalties, promoted officers on merit, adopted a written script for the Mongol language and issued a body of law, the *yassa*. The armies that resulted took northern China, Central Asia and Persia within two decades; the [campaigns](item:mongol-conquests) were highly destructive, and the sack of cities that resisted was policy rather than accident.

The empire he left reached from Korea to the Caspian and, under his successors, from Hungary to the Pacific. Mongol control of the [trade routes across Eurasia](item:silk-roads) moved goods, techniques and, in all likelihood, the plague that became the [Black Death](item:black-death). His burial place is unknown.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genghis_Khan).

name: Mongol conquests
summary: The largest contiguous land empire in history was assembled in three generations, from Korea to Hungary.
body:
The Mongol conquests were the campaigns by which Genghis Khan and his descendants assembled the largest contiguous land empire in history, reaching from Korea to the Danube and from Siberia to the Persian Gulf. They ran from the [proclamation of Genghis Khan](event:genghis-khan) in 1206 to the death of his grandson Kublai in 1294, by which time the empire had already broken into four rival khanates.

Mongol forces were usually smaller than those they faced, but were composed almost entirely of mounted archers who could move at a pace their enemies could not match, were organised in decimal units that cut across tribal loyalty, and were held to an unusually harsh discipline. They learned siege warfare from Chinese and Muslim engineers taken into their service, which is what allowed steppe cavalry to reduce walled cities. Terror was used deliberately: a city that resisted after being summoned to surrender could expect to be destroyed and its people killed, and word of that made the next city surrender.

The destruction was real and in places demographic. The irrigation works of Persia and the cities of Khwarazm did not recover for centuries, and the [sack of Baghdad](event:baghdad-1258) in 1258 ended five centuries of Abbasid caliphate. The figures the chroniclers give for the dead are not credible as arithmetic, and modern estimates are much lower.

One authority from the Black Sea to the Pacific then made the overland routes safe enough that merchants, envoys, missionaries and craftsmen crossed Eurasia in numbers, [Marco Polo](event:marco-polo) among them, carrying goods, techniques and, in all likelihood, the plague that became the [Black Death](event:black-death). Chinese gunpowder and printing, Persian astronomy and Islamic medicine all travelled the same roads.

The empire could not hold itself together. Succession was decided by assembly and every one of them was contested; after the civil war of 1260–64 the four khanates, the [Yuan](event:yuan-dynasty) in China, the Chagatai in Central Asia, the Ilkhanate in Persia and the Golden Horde on the steppe, went their own ways, adopted the religions and the administrations of the people they ruled, and fought each other.

The campaigns are listed as steps.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_conquests).

steps.name: Western Xia and the Jin
steps.page: The first campaigns were against the two states on the Mongols' southern border. The Tangut kingdom of Western Xia was raided from 1209 and destroyed in 1227. The Jin empire of northern China was attacked from 1211; its capital Zhongdu, on the site of modern Beijing, fell in 1215 after a siege and was burnt. The Jin held out south of the Yellow River until 1234. These wars gave the Mongols engineers, siege equipment and administrators.

steps.name: The Khwarazmian campaign
steps.page: The shah of Khwarazm had a Mongol trade caravan killed and then executed the envoys sent to complain. The response destroyed his empire in two years. Bukhara, Samarkand, Urgench, Merv and Nishapur were taken and their populations killed or enslaved; the shah died a fugitive on an island in the Caspian. A detachment under Jebe and Subutai rode on round the Caspian, beat a Rus' and Cuman army at the Kalka river in 1223, and returned by way of the steppe.

steps.name: The death of Genghis Khan
steps.page: Genghis Khan died in August 1227, campaigning again against Western Xia. His burial place was deliberately concealed and has never been found. The empire passed, after two years of regency, to his third son Ögedei, who was elected at a *kurultai* in 1229 and built a capital at Karakorum. Succession by assembly rather than by rule was the flaw that eventually broke the empire apart.

steps.name: The western campaign
steps.page: An army under Batu, Genghis's grandson, with Subutai directing the operations, crossed the Volga in 1236. Volga Bulgaria, Ryazan, Vladimir and finally Kiev in December 1240 were taken and destroyed; the Rus' principalities became tributaries of what became the Golden Horde. In 1241 two Mongol forces beat a Polish and German army at Legnica and the Hungarian army at Mohi within two days of each other. They withdrew from central Europe in 1242, after news arrived that Ögedei had died.

steps.name: Checked at Ain Jalut
steps.page: On 3 September 1260, at Ain Jalut in Galilee, a Mamluk army from Egypt destroyed a Mongol force that Hulagu had left behind when he withdrew east with the bulk of his troops. It was the first strategic defeat the Mongols had suffered, and it fixed the western limit of their expansion at the Euphrates. The Mamluk sultanate that won it went on to take the last of the crusader states.

steps.name: The conquest of Song China
steps.page: The Southern Song were the hardest of the Mongols' opponents, and took forty years to break. The double fortress of Xiangyang on the Han river held out from 1268 to 1273 and fell only to counterweight trebuchets built by engineers brought from Persia. Hangzhou, the largest city in the world, surrendered in 1276; the last Song loyalists were destroyed at the naval battle of Yamen in 1279, where an official is said to have jumped into the sea carrying the child emperor.

steps.name: The invasions of Japan
steps.page: Kublai sent two seaborne invasions against Japan, in 1274 and in 1281. The second was much the larger; the sources describe some 4,000 ships and 140,000 men, in two fleets from Korea and southern China. Both were held on the beaches of Kyushu by the defenders and then wrecked by typhoons, which Japanese tradition named *kamikaze*, divine winds. Campaigns against Vietnam, Champa and Java also failed.

steps.name: Four khanates
steps.page: Kublai died in 1294 as emperor of China and nominal Great Khan of an empire that no longer acknowledged him. The Golden Horde, the Chagatai khanate and the Ilkhanate were by then independent states, at war with one another as often as with anybody else, and each was being absorbed by the culture it governed: the Ilkhans and the Horde became Muslim, the Yuan Chinese. The unified empire had lasted a little under ninety years.

name: Black Death
summary: The deadliest pandemic in recorded history killed between a third and a half of the population of Europe between 1346 and 1353.
body:
The Black Death was a pandemic of plague that killed a large part of the population of Europe, western Asia and North Africa between 1346 and 1353. Estimates of the European death toll range from a quarter to two thirds of the population; a third to a half is the usual figure, and Europe did not return to its earlier numbers for about two hundred years. It is the deadliest pandemic in recorded history.

The disease was caused by the bacterium *Yersinia pestis*, which was not identified until Alexandre Yersin isolated it during an outbreak in Hong Kong in 1894. Genetic work on medieval burials has since confirmed it in the fourteenth-century dead and traced the strain's ancestor to Central Asia, where tombstones in the Chu valley of present-day Kyrgyzstan record a spike in deaths from "pestilence" in 1338 and 1339. How it then spread is still argued about: the classic account has it carried by rat fleas, while more recent work holds that the speed of the medieval spread fits human fleas, body lice and person-to-person pneumonic transmission better.

It reached Europe along the trade routes. Plague was in the Golden Horde army besieging the Genoese port of Caffa in Crimea in 1346, and Genoese ships carried it to Constantinople in the summer of 1347 and to Sicily that October. From the Italian ports it took about three years to cross the continent, moving faster along coasts and rivers than overland.

Nobody knew what it was. Explanations ran from a conjunction of the planets to corrupted air to divine punishment, and the responses from quarantine (Ragusa's thirty-day isolation of arriving ships in 1377 gave the word its name) to flagellant processions and to the massacre of Jewish communities accused of poisoning wells.

The demographic shock rearranged the economy. Land was suddenly plentiful and labour scarce; wages rose, rents fell, and attempts to legislate wages back down met resistance, of which the English rising of 1381 was one instance. Serfdom weakened across much of western Europe, and plague itself did not go away: it returned in waves every decade or two for three hundred years.

Its course across Europe is traced in the steps.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death).

steps.name: The siege of Caffa
steps.page: Plague was already moving west along the caravan routes from Central Asia when it reached the army of Jani Beg, khan of the Golden Horde, besieging the Genoese trading colony of Caffa in the Crimea. The chronicler Gabriele de' Mussi, writing at second hand, says the besiegers catapulted their own dead over the walls; historians treat the detail with caution but not the outbreak. Genoese ships left the port for home.

steps.name: Constantinople and the Black Sea
steps.page: The disease arrived in Constantinople in the summer of 1347, the first place in Europe it is recorded. The emperor John VI Kantakouzenos, whose own son died of it, wrote a description of the symptoms modelled on Thucydides. From the Bosphorus it went with shipping in every direction at once: to the Aegean, to Alexandria, and westward along the Mediterranean sea lanes.

steps.name: Twelve galleys at Messina
steps.page: In October 1347 twelve Genoese galleys put in at Messina in Sicily with dying crews. The town expelled them, which spread the infection along the coast rather than containing it, and the whole island was affected within months. Sicily is the entry point from which the pandemic's course through western Europe is usually traced.

steps.name: Alexandria, Cairo and the Levant
steps.page: Ships out of the Black Sea carried plague to Alexandria in the autumn of 1347, and from there it went up the Nile and across the Levant. Cairo, then one of the largest cities in the world, is reported to have lost between a third and two fifths of its people within eight months. Mortality across the Middle East is generally put at about a third, comparable to the European figure.

steps.name: Genoa, Venice, Pisa and Marseille
steps.page: Galleys from Caffa reached Genoa and Venice in January 1348. The outbreak that followed a few weeks later at Pisa was the entry into northern Italy, and one of the ships driven out of an Italian harbour carried the plague to Marseille at the end of the same month. Florence, whose losses Boccaccio described in the introduction to the *Decameron*, fell from something over 110,000 people to about 50,000 by 1351.

steps.name: France, Iberia and England
steps.page: From Marseille the plague went up the Rhône to Avignon, where the pope's physician Guy de Chauliac stayed and wrote about it, and across Languedoc into Spain. It reached the south coast of England in the summer of 1348 and London by the autumn. Paris is estimated to have lost half of its hundred thousand people. Governments responded chiefly by trying to hold wages and prices where they had been.

steps.name: Attacks on Jewish communities
steps.page: From late 1348 a rumour that Jews had poisoned the wells spread through the Rhineland, Alsace, Switzerland and the Empire, in several places arriving before the plague itself did. Whole communities were burnt or expelled; about two thousand people were killed at Strasbourg in February 1349, before the plague had reached the town at all. Pope Clement VI issued two bulls against the accusation and could not stop it. Many survivors migrated east into Poland and Lithuania.

steps.name: Germany, Scotland and Scandinavia
steps.page: Through 1349 and 1350 the plague worked north and east through the German lands, into Scotland, and by sea to Scandinavia: a ship put in at Askøy in 1349 and the outbreak spread from Bjørgvin, modern Bergen, over the whole of Norway. Hamburg and Bremen are each thought to have lost at least three fifths of their inhabitants. Iceland and Greenland were reached later or, in Greenland's case, perhaps not at all.

steps.name: Northern Russia and Moscow
steps.page: The pandemic completed a circuit. Having entered Europe from the Black Sea, it arrived in northern Russia only in 1352, reaching Novgorod and Pskov by way of the Baltic, and Moscow in 1353, where it killed the grand prince and his family. That is the conventional end of the first wave. Plague returned to Europe in 1361, in 1374, and every decade or two thereafter until the eighteenth century.

name: The Renaissance
summary: A revival of classical learning and a transformation of European art, architecture and thought, beginning in Florence.
body:
The Renaissance was a period of European cultural change, running roughly from the fourteenth century to the early seventeenth, in which the art, literature and learning of Greek and Roman antiquity were recovered, imitated and eventually surpassed. It began in the city-states of northern Italy, above all Florence, and spread across the continent. The name means rebirth and was applied to the period by nineteenth-century historians.

Its intellectual programme was humanism: the study of grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and moral philosophy from ancient sources read in the original, rather than through medieval commentary. Petrarch hunted lost manuscripts in monastic libraries; scholars learned Greek from Byzantine teachers and from refugees after [the fall of Constantinople](event:fall-constantinople) in 1453; Lorenzo Valla proved the Donation of Constantine a forgery by examining its Latin, which is textual criticism recognisably modern. Cheap books from [the printing press](event:printing-press) carried the results everywhere.

In art the change was technical as much as intellectual. Linear perspective was worked out by Brunelleschi and set down by Alberti; anatomy was studied by dissection; oil paint, developed in the Netherlands, allowed depth of colour and detail that tempera could not. The subjects remained largely religious, but the treatment was of individual human beings standing in a coherent space. [Leonardo](item:leonardo-da-vinci), Michelangelo, Raphael, Titian, Dürer and Bruegel all worked within a century of one another.

Florentine bankers, Venetian merchants, the dukes of Milan, Ferrara and Urbino, the kings of France and England, and the popes competed for artists as a form of politics. Julius II and Leo X between them commissioned the new St Peter's, the [Sistine ceiling](event:sistine-chapel) and Raphael's rooms.

The period was not a golden age for everybody in it: it contained plague, war, the sack of Rome in 1527, the witch trials, and the religious wars that followed the [Reformation](event:reformation). Historians have long questioned the sharp break the name implies, since the twelfth century had a recovery of ancient learning of its own.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance).

name: Age of Discovery
summary: European ships opened sea routes to Africa, Asia and the Americas, joining the world's hemispheres into a single system.
body:
The Age of Discovery is the name given to the period, roughly from the early fifteenth century to the early seventeenth, in which European ships found and mapped sea routes to Africa, Asia and the Americas. It joined hemispheres that had been effectively separate since the end of the last ice age, and it began the European maritime empires.

Portugal started it, for reasons of position and of politics. The capture of Ceuta in 1415 gave a foothold in Morocco; from the 1420s expeditions sponsored by [Prince Henry](event:henry-navigator) worked south along the Atlantic coast of Africa, settling Madeira and the Azores and passing Cape Bojador in 1434, a limit sailors had believed impassable. Each voyage went a little further and came back with gold, pepper and enslaved people. The caravel, lateen-rigged and able to beat back north against the prevailing winds, made the return journey possible; the quadrant, the astrolabe and tables of solar declination made latitude calculable.

[Dias](event:dias) rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488 and [da Gama](event:da-gama) reached Calicut ten years later. [Columbus](event:columbus), sailing west for Spain on a serious underestimate of the size of the Earth, made landfall in the Bahamas in 1492 and never accepted that it was not Asia. [Magellan's expedition](event:magellan) crossed the Pacific, and one of its ships came home in 1522 having gone round.

The consequences differed by region. Europe gained world maps, new crops, bullion and a lead in armed shipping. In the Americas the voyages were followed by [conquest](event:spanish-conquest) and by [epidemics](event:americas-epidemics) that killed most of the population within a century. In Africa they were followed by four hundred years of the [Atlantic slave trade](event:slave-trade), and in Asia by armed European trading posts that later became colonies. The [Columbian Exchange](event:columbian-exchange) of crops, animals and diseases changed diets and populations everywhere.

The voyages are listed as steps.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Discovery).

steps.name: Past Cape Bojador
steps.page: Cape Bojador, on the Saharan coast south of the Canaries, was where the Portuguese effort stopped for a decade. The current sets south and the wind blows south, so a ship that went beyond it might not get back, and sailors said the sea boiled there. Gil Eanes passed it in 1434 by standing out to sea and returning on a wide westward arc, the manoeuvre later called the *volta do mar*, which was used on every later Atlantic route.

steps.name: The Guinea coast
steps.page: After Henry's death the crown leased the African trade to merchants and then took it back. Ships reached the Gold Coast in the 1470s, where the fort of São Jorge da Mina was built in 1482 to hold the gold trade, and crossed the equator soon after. Diogo Cão found the mouth of the Congo in 1483. The coast was measured as it went: stone *padrões* were set up at the furthest point of each voyage, and the pilots' latitude tables were corrected once the Pole Star dropped below the horizon.

steps.name: Dias rounds the Cape of Good Hope
The Portuguese in the Indian Ocean
steps.page: Portugal followed the route with fleets. Cabral, blown or steered west on the way to India in 1500, made landfall in Brazil and claimed it. Afonso de Albuquerque then took the choke points rather than the territory: Goa in 1510, Malacca in 1511, Hormuz in 1515, with an attempt on Aden that failed. It was a trading empire held by fortresses and gunnery, and for a century it controlled the sea route between Europe and Asia.

steps.name: The first circumnavigation
steps.page: Five ships under Ferdinand Magellan left Spain in 1519 to reach the spice islands by sailing west. They found the strait at the foot of South America, crossed a Pacific far wider than anyone had imagined, and lost most of their crews to starvation and scurvy; Magellan was killed in the Philippines. One ship, the *Victoria*, came home in 1522 under Juan Sebastián Elcano with eighteen men aboard, having sailed round the world and settled the argument about its size.

steps.name: The Pacific and the northern routes
steps.page: The return route across the Pacific was found in 1565, which made the Manila galleon possible and tied American silver to Chinese markets for two and a half centuries. English and Dutch ships entered waters the treaty of 1494 had assigned elsewhere: Drake went round the world between 1577 and 1580, and expeditions searched for north-west and north-east passages that did not exist in any usable form. By 1600 the outline of the inhabited world, apart from Australia and the Pacific interior, was on European charts.

name: Gutenberg's printing press
summary: Gutenberg's movable metal type made books cheap and made it far harder to suppress an idea once it had spread.
body:
The printing press with movable metal type was assembled by [Johannes Gutenberg](item:johannes-gutenberg) at Mainz in the 1440s. Within fifty years presses were working in more than two hundred European towns and had produced something like twenty million books, more than all the scribes of the previous thousand years together.

No single part of it was new. [Block printing](event:woodblock-printing) had come from China, [metal type](event:korea-movable-type) had been cast in Korea two centuries earlier, and the screw press was borrowed from wine and oil making. What Gutenberg put together was a system: a hand mould that cast thousands of identical letters in a lead-tin-antimony alloy quickly and to a uniform height, an oil-based ink that would hold to metal instead of beading on it, and a press that applied even pressure across a whole forme at once. Each part had to work for the others to be worth anything.

A printed book cost a fraction of a manuscript, and the cost per copy fell with the length of the run, so printers had to find markets. They found them in universities, churches, courts, merchants' offices and eventually households. Latin gave way to the vernaculars as the audience widened; spelling and grammar hardened as texts were reproduced identically; title pages, page numbers, indexes and errata appeared because they had become useful.

Its political effect was that an idea in print could not be recalled. Luther's tracts made the [Reformation](event:reformation) a European event within months rather than a local dispute; identical diagrams and tables let natural philosophers across the continent build on one another's results, which the [Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution) required; and governments answered with censorship, licensing and privilege systems.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press).

name: Printing
summary: The reproduction of text and images by mechanical means, which made copies of a text cheap to produce in quantity.
body:
Printing is older than the printing press. [Woodblock printing](item:woodblock-printing) was in use in Tang China by the seventh century, and [movable type](item:korea-movable-type), ceramic under the Song and metal in Goryeo Korea by 1234, preceded Europe by two centuries. What limited them was the script: a font of Chinese characters runs to thousands of sorts, and a scribe was often the cheaper option.

An alphabet changes that arithmetic, and [Gutenberg's](item:johannes-gutenberg) combination of a type mould, oil-based ink and the [screw press](item:printing-press) made the copying of a book a matter of hours. The [42-line Bible](item:gutenberg-42-line) demonstrated it; by 1500 some 20 million volumes had been printed in Europe.

An idea in print could not be suppressed by burning one copy, which is part of why the [Reformation](item:reformation) spread as it did; standardised texts made the [Scientific Revolution's](item:scientific-revolution) accumulation of results possible; and fixed spellings and vernacular Bibles hardened national languages.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_printing).

name: Leonardo da Vinci
summary: Florentine painter, engineer and anatomist whose notebooks and few finished paintings define the range of the Italian Renaissance.
body:
Leonardo was the illegitimate son of a notary, apprenticed at about fourteen to Andrea del Verrocchio in Florence. He worked for the Sforza in Milan, for Cesare Borgia as a military engineer, for the Republic of Florence and finally for Francis I of France, who gave him a manor house near Amboise.

He finished very little. *The Last Supper* and the [*Mona Lisa*](item:mona-lisa) are among perhaps fifteen surviving paintings, and both changed how European artists handled gesture, atmosphere and the modelling of light.

His notebooks, some 7,000 surviving pages in mirror writing, range over anatomy from dissection, the flight of birds, water, geology, optics and machines from a diving suit to a helical rotor. Almost none of it was published in his lifetime, so its influence on later science was slight.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci).

name: Fall of Constantinople
summary: Ottoman cannon breached the Theodosian walls and the last Roman emperor died fighting; the Byzantine Empire ended after 1,100 years.
body:
Constantinople fell to the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II on 29 May 1453, after a siege of fifty-three days. The last Roman emperor, Constantine XI, was killed in the fighting and his body was never identified. The empire that had governed from the city since 330 ended with him, 1,123 years after Constantine I founded it.

The city had never recovered from the [Fourth Crusade's](event:fourth-crusade) sack in 1204, its territory had shrunk to the walls and a few outposts, and perhaps 50,000 people lived among fields and ruins in a city built for many times that. The Theodosian walls, though, had turned back every attacker for a thousand years.

Mehmed brought between 50,000 and 80,000 men against fewer than 8,000 defenders, and a siege train that included a bombard cast by the Hungarian engineer Orban which threw a stone ball of over half a tonne. The defence of the land walls was directed by the Genoese commander Giovanni Giustiniani. The siege ran in phases, from the first bombardment through the moving of a fleet overland into the Golden Horn to the assault of 29 May; the steps follow them in order.

Mehmed entered the city that day, allowed the customary three days of plunder and then stopped it early, and made Constantinople his capital. Hagia Sophia became a mosque. He repopulated the city by resettlement and confirmed the Orthodox patriarch in office as head of his Christian subjects.

Europe received the news as a catastrophe. It helped push Greek scholars and manuscripts west into the [Renaissance](event:renaissance), and Ottoman control of the land routes east is part of the reason European states began looking for [a sea route to Asia](event:age-of-discovery).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople).

steps.name: The army before the walls
steps.page:
Ottoman troops appeared before the land walls on 2 April 1453 and Mehmed II arrived with the main body on 5 April. Estimates of his army run from 50,000 to 80,000 men, against rather under 8,000 defenders for a perimeter of some twenty kilometres.

The defenders drew the great chain across the mouth of the Golden Horn, closing the harbour to the Ottoman fleet. Mehmed placed his own tent opposite the Mesoteichion, the middle stretch of wall where the Lycus stream crosses the line and the ground is lowest. Karaca Pasha took the northern sector, Ishak Pasha the ground from the Lycus down to the Marmara.

layers.label: The chain across the Golden Horn
Ottoman fleet at the Double Columns

steps.name: The bombardment opens
steps.page:
The siege proper began on 6 April, when the guns opened on the land walls. The largest was cast at Edirne by the Hungarian founder Orban and threw a stone ball of over half a tonne; it could be fired only a few times a day.

The batteries concentrated on the Mesoteichion and on the Charisius gate. Sections of the outer wall were brought down and rebuilt at night with earth, rubble and barrels, and the defenders held the repaired stockade rather than the breach. A general assault on 18 April was thrown back after several hours.

steps.name: Four ships reach the Horn
steps.page:
On 20 April three Genoese ships carrying men and supplies from the pope, and one imperial transport carrying grain, met the Ottoman fleet off the city. The Ottoman vessels were smaller and lower and could not board the tall Genoese carracks.

The fight was watched from both shores. The four ships worked through, the chain was opened to let them into the Golden Horn, and Mehmed removed the fleet commander Baltaoglu. The action showed that the harbour could not be forced while the chain held.

steps.name: Ships hauled into the Golden Horn
steps.page:
On 22 April Mehmed had about seventy vessels dragged out of the Bosphorus and hauled on greased rollers over the ridge behind Galata, then launched into the Golden Horn above the chain. The Genoese of Pera, formally neutral, did not stop the work.

A fleet inside the harbour put the low sea walls along the Horn under threat and forced the defenders to spread their small numbers further. An attempt to burn the ships with fire ships on 28 April failed, and the captured survivors were executed within sight of the walls.

steps.name: Mines and the siege tower
steps.page:
Between 16 and 25 May Ottoman sappers, many of them Saxon silver miners from Serbia, drove tunnels under the walls in the Blachernae sector. The defenders located them by countermining under the direction of the engineer Johannes Grant, and flooded, burned or fought them out underground.

A wheeled siege tower brought up against the Caligaria gate on 18 May was destroyed the following night. A partial lunar eclipse on 22 May and heavy rain in the days after were read in the city as omens.

steps.name: The last days
steps.page:
Mehmed offered terms which would have left Constantine XI a ruler in the Morea if the city were surrendered; the offer was refused. On 26 and 27 May the Ottoman camp prepared for a general assault, and fires were lit along the lines.

The defenders spent 28 May repairing the stockade at the Lycus and carrying icons in procession through the streets. A service was held in Hagia Sophia that evening, attended by both Orthodox and Latin clergy. The gates behind the outer wall were locked so that the garrison could not fall back.

steps.name: The final assault
steps.page:
The assault began shortly after midnight on 29 May and came in three waves: irregular azaps first, then Anatolian regiments, then the janissaries. The weight fell on the Mesoteichion, with attacks on the Blachernae walls and from the ships in the Horn.

Giovanni Giustiniani, who commanded the defence of the land walls, was wounded and carried off through the inner wall, and the stockade gave way behind him. A small postern, the Kerkoporta, was found open near Blachernae and Ottoman troops came through it. Constantine XI was killed in the fighting and his body was not identified. Mehmed entered the city that day and made it his capital.

name: Columbus reaches the Americas
summary: Between 1492 and 1504 Christopher Columbus led four Spanish expeditions across the Atlantic to the Americas. The first made landfall in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). Between 1492 and 1504 the Italian explorer and navigator Christopher Columbus led four Spanish transatlantic expeditions to the Americas in the name of the Catholic Monarchs. On 12 October 1492, thirty-six days out from the Canary Islands, the first of them made landfall on an island in the Bahamas that Columbus named San Salvador. He believed he had reached the outlying islands of Asia and held to that view for the rest of his life, which is why the Caribbean came to be called the West Indies.

Columbus was looking for a western sea route to the East Indies and its spice trade. He took a small estimate of the circumference of the Earth and a large one of the eastward extent of Asia, and placed Japan about 4,500 kilometres west of the Canaries. Portuguese advisers rejected the calculation, correctly. After the [war for Granada](event:granada) ended, Isabella I and Ferdinand II agreed to fund the voyage on terms granting him the titles of admiral, viceroy and governor of any lands he found.

The first voyage left Palos de la Frontera in August 1492 with the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña, visited the Bahamas, Cuba and Hispaniola, and left thirty-nine men at La Navidad after the Santa María was wrecked on Christmas Day. The second, from 1493 to 1496, sailed with seventeen ships, founded La Isabela on Hispaniola and imposed tribute and forced labour on the Taíno. The third, from 1498 to 1500, reached Trinidad and the Orinoco delta, the first recorded European sighting of the South American mainland; complaints from colonists and reports of his government of Hispaniola led the crown to remove him as governor and send him back to Spain in chains. The fourth, from 1502 to 1504, followed the coast of Central America.

The Taíno population of Hispaniola fell steeply within a generation under warfare, forced labour and introduced disease. [Norse voyagers](event:vinland) had reached Newfoundland about five centuries earlier, but that contact did not continue. The voyages were followed by the [Columbian Exchange](event:columbian-exchange), the [Spanish conquest of the mainland](event:spanish-conquest), the [epidemics](event:americas-epidemics) that killed most of the hemisphere's inhabitants, and sustained European colonisation of the Americas.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyages_of_Christopher_Columbus).

name: The Columbian Exchange
summary: Crops, animals and diseases moved between the hemispheres after 1492, transforming diets and populations on every continent.
body:
The Columbian Exchange is the name given to the transfer of crops, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492. The historian Alfred Crosby coined the term in 1972. It is one of the largest biological events in human history, and its effects on diet and population were felt on every continent.

Disease moved chiefly in one direction. Smallpox, measles, typhus, influenza and later yellow fever entered populations with no acquired immunity to any of them and killed, on most estimates, between two thirds and nine tenths of the pre-contact population of the Americas within a century and a half. That collapse is inseparable from the European conquests: the [epidemics](event:americas-epidemics) ran ahead of the armies in many places, and the states that fell had often already lost their rulers and much of their administration.

Food crops moved chiefly the other way. Maize, potatoes, sweet potatoes, cassava, beans, tomatoes, peppers, squash, cacao, groundnuts, pineapple and tobacco were unknown outside the Americas in 1491. Potatoes and maize yield far more calories per hectare than the grains they came to supplement in Europe, Africa and China, and the population growth of the following centuries, which supplied the workforce of the [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution), depended on them. Cassava and maize became staples across much of Africa.

Traffic in the other direction included wheat, rice, sugar cane, bananas, coffee, cattle, pigs, sheep, chickens and the horse, which transformed societies on the plains of both American continents. Sugar and coffee were then grown in the Americas by enslaved Africans carried across in the [Atlantic slave trade](event:slave-trade).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbian_exchange).

name: Protestant Reformation
summary: The Reformation split Western Christianity. From Martin Luther's protest against indulgences in 1517, reformers rejected papal authority and much of Catholic doctrine, and within a generation much of northern Europe had left the Roman church. The division ran through European politics as well as religion, and the wars connected with it continued until 1648.
body:
Much of the criticism was old: clerical wealth, absentee bishops, the sale of pardons and the papacy's temporal power had been attacked for two centuries. What was new was reach. The [printing press](event:printing-press) carried Luther's tracts across Germany in weeks, vernacular Bibles put the text in lay hands, and princes who wanted church lands and independence from the emperor had reasons of their own to protect him.

It was never one movement. Luther held to a real presence in the Eucharist that Zwingli denied, and the two failed to agree at Marburg in 1529. Anabaptists rejected infant baptism and were persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike. Calvin's Geneva produced a disciplined church order that spread to France, Scotland, the Netherlands and the Rhine. England's break was made by a king for dynastic reasons and given a Protestant content afterwards. Catholic reform answered at the Council of Trent, which restated doctrine without concession and tightened clerical discipline, and in new orders, above all the Jesuits.

The settlement was fought over for a century and a quarter: in Germany, in the French wars of religion, in the [Dutch Revolt](event:netherlands-independence), and finally in the [Thirty Years' War](event:thirty-years-war). The [Peace of Westphalia](event:westphalia) of 1648 ended the fighting by conceding that Europe would stay divided. Religious allegiance was settled thereafter by the sovereign state rather than by a universal church, and the confessional map of Europe drawn in these years is still largely in place.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation).

steps.name: The Diet of Worms
steps.page:
Summoned before Charles V and the imperial diet at Worms in April 1521, Luther was shown his books and asked to retract them. He refused unless convinced by scripture or plain reason, and was given safe conduct home.

The Edict of Worms in May declared him an outlaw whom anyone might kill without penalty, and banned his writings. The Elector of Saxony had him taken to the Wartburg instead, where he translated the New Testament into German.

steps.name: The German Peasants' War
steps.page:
Peasants and townsmen across southern and central Germany rose from 1524, citing the gospel against serfdom, tithes and hunting rights; the Twelve Articles of Memmingen were among the first printed statements of popular grievance in Europe.

Luther, whose language they had borrowed, denounced them and urged the princes to strike. Perhaps 100,000 were killed. The reformation of the church was decisively attached to the authority of the princes rather than to the commons.

steps.name: The Augsburg Confession
steps.page:
Melanchthon's statement of Lutheran doctrine was read to the emperor at the diet of Augsburg in June 1530. It was drafted to look as little heretical as possible, and it remains the confessional basis of Lutheran churches.

Rejected by the Catholic side, it hardened the division into two organised parties and led directly to the defensive Schmalkaldic League of Protestant princes.

steps.name: Calvin's Geneva
steps.page:
John Calvin returned to Geneva in 1541 and built a church order of pastors, teachers, elders and deacons, with a consistory that supervised belief and conduct. His *Institutes of the Christian Religion*, revised through his life, became the most systematic statement of Reformed theology.

The city took in refugees and printed for export. Reformed churches on the Genevan model spread to France, Scotland, the Netherlands and the Rhineland.

name: Spanish conquest of the Americas
summary: Between 1519 and 1572 Spanish expeditions overthrew the Aztec and Inca empires and claimed most of the Americas for the crown of Castile. Small Spanish forces succeeded through firearms, horses and steel, through alliances with peoples subject to those empires, and through epidemic disease that had arrived ahead of them.
body:
Conquest was carried out by licensed private ventures rather than royal armies: a leader raised men and money on credit and was paid in a share of the loot and in *encomiendas*, grants of Indigenous labour. Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico in 1519 with about 500 men and took [Tenochtitlan](event:tenochtitlan) in 1521 with tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan allies. Francisco Pizarro seized the Inca emperor Atahualpa in 1532, at a moment when the [Inca](event:inca-conquest) were emerging from a war of succession between two brothers, and held Cusco by the end of 1533.

Neither conquest was quick or complete. Maya polities in Yucatán and Guatemala resisted for decades, and the last independent one, Nojpetén, fell only in 1697; a rump Inca state held out at Vilcabamba until 1572; the Mapuche of southern Chile were never subdued. Rebellion and the collapse of the Indigenous population made the conquered lands hard to hold and harder to tax.

What replaced the old empires was a colonial order of viceroyalties, Catholic missions, cathedral cities and silver mines. Bullion from [Potosí](event:potosi-silver) and Zacatecas financed Habsburg Spain and reached China aboard the [Manila galleons](event:manila-galleon). The crown legislated repeatedly against the worst abuses under pressure from clerics such as [Las Casas](event:las-casas), with limited effect at the distance involved.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_colonization_of_the_Americas).

steps.name: Cortés lands in Mexico
steps.page:
Hernán Cortés landed near modern Veracruz in April 1519 with about 500 men, sixteen horses and a few guns, in defiance of the governor of Cuba who had tried to recall him. He founded a town, had it elect him, and so claimed to answer to the king alone.

He beached his ships to stop anyone returning, and marched inland gathering allies among the Totonacs and then the Tlaxcalans, who fought him hard before joining him.

steps.name: The Maya campaigns
steps.page:
Pedro de Alvarado moved into Guatemala in 1524 and Francisco de Montejo into Yucatán from 1527. Neither found a single capital to capture: Maya political power was divided among many kingdoms, in country that suited defenders.

Yucatán took nearly twenty years and two abandoned attempts before Mérida was founded in 1542 and the north subdued by 1546. The last independent Maya state, Nojpetén in the Petén lakes, held out until 1697.

steps.name: The New Laws
steps.page:
Pressed by [Las Casas](event:las-casas) and by the Council of the Indies, Charles V issued laws in November 1542 forbidding the enslavement of Indigenous people, limiting the *encomienda* and ending its inheritance.

The colonists rebelled. A viceroy sent to enforce the laws in Peru was defeated and beheaded in 1546, and the inheritance clause was repealed. The crown had asserted that the conquered were its subjects rather than the conquerors' property, and had shown how little it could enforce at that distance.

steps.name: The last Inca state falls
steps.page:
A rump Inca state had survived since 1537 in the forested mountains at Vilcabamba, north-west of Cusco, under Manco Inca and his sons. It raided the highways and sheltered those who would not submit.

Viceroy Toledo sent an expedition in 1572. Vilcabamba was burned, and the last Inca, Túpac Amaru, was brought to Cusco and beheaded in the square before a crowd that is said to have begged for his life. Toledo's reorganisation of labour and settlement followed.

name: Epidemics devastate the Americas
summary: Old World diseases reached the Americas with Europeans and killed most of the Indigenous population within a century. Smallpox, measles, typhus and unidentified fevers often spread far ahead of settlers. Estimates of the overall decline run from about 80 to 95 per cent, and they vary widely because the pre-contact population is itself disputed.
body:
Part of [The Columbian Exchange](event:columbian-exchange). Populations separated from Eurasia and Africa for thousands of years had no acquired immunity to smallpox, measles, influenza, typhus or malaria, and the diseases arrived together rather than one at a time, so that a society weakened by one outbreak met the next before it had recovered. Epidemics moved along Indigenous trade and tribute routes, which meant that many peoples were struck before they had seen a European at all.

Disease was not the whole of it. War, enslavement, forced labour in mines and fields, the seizure of stored food, the disruption of planting and the breakdown of households with nobody well enough to fetch water made each outbreak far deadlier than the pathogen alone would have been. In most regions the population did not begin to recover until the eighteenth century.

The scale of the depopulation may even be readable in the atmosphere: one much-discussed study argues that forest regrowing on abandoned farmland drew down enough carbon dioxide to register in Antarctic ice cores around 1610. Arguments of that kind depend on pre-contact population figures that specialists still dispute by a factor of several.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_history_of_Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas).

steps.name: Smallpox reaches Mexico
steps.page:
Smallpox came ashore with a Spanish expedition in 1520 and reached the Valley of Mexico while the war with Cortés was under way. It killed the emperor Cuitláhuac and a large share of the population of [Tenochtitlan](event:tenochtitlan) during the siege.

From there it spread through Mesoamerica along established trade and tribute routes, reaching Guatemala by 1521, where the Kaqchikel annals record it independently of any European presence.

steps.name: Smallpox in the Andes
steps.page:
The epidemic ran ahead of the Spanish down the Andes and reached the Inca empire several years before Pizarro did. It killed the emperor Huayna Capac and his designated heir.

The succession war between Atahualpa and Huáscar that followed is what left the empire divided when the [Spanish arrived](event:inca-conquest) in 1532.

steps.name: Measles through Central America
steps.page:
A measles epidemic swept New Spain and Central America in the early 1530s, striking populations already thinned by smallpox and by the labour demands of conquest.

Compound outbreaks of this kind, with one disease arriving before a society had recovered from the last, are what made the American mortality so much higher than any single European epidemic.

steps.name: The cocoliztli of 1545
steps.page:
The deadliest epidemic recorded in the Americas began in 1545 and lasted three years. Nahua sources call it *cocoliztli*, a haemorrhagic fever with high fatality that affected Indigenous people far more than Spaniards.

Estimates of the dead across New Spain run to several million, with some 800,000 in the Valley of Mexico alone. Its cause is still argued over; one line of research points to an enteric fever, another to a native rodent-borne virus made worse by drought and forced labour.

steps.name: The Brazilian coast
steps.page:
Smallpox and an unidentified epidemic ran through the Tupi peoples of the Brazilian coast and the Jesuit mission villages in the early 1560s, together with a famine caused when nobody was well enough to plant.

The collapse of coastal Indigenous labour is one reason Portuguese sugar planters turned to importing enslaved Africans on a large scale.

steps.name: The cocoliztli of 1576
steps.page:
A second great cocoliztli epidemic ran from 1576 to about 1580 and killed perhaps two million people. It is far better documented than the first: the physician Francisco Hernández performed autopsies and left a clinical description.

By its end the Indigenous population of central Mexico was a small fraction of what it had been in 1519, and the colonial economy was being rebuilt around that fact.

name: Transatlantic slave trade
summary: Between the sixteenth century and the 1860s, European and American ships carried about 12.5 million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic; some 10.7 million survived the crossing. It was the largest forced migration in history, and it supplied the labour for the plantation economies of Brazil, the Caribbean and North America.
body:
Captives were bought on the African coast, mostly from African rulers and merchants who obtained them through war, raiding and judicial enslavement inland, in exchange for textiles, metalware, firearms and alcohol. They were held in coastal forts and barracoons and then packed below decks for the Middle Passage, a voyage of six to twelve weeks in which roughly one in eight died of dysentery, smallpox and dehydration. Ships carried plantation produce back to Europe, the triangle the trade is usually drawn as, though many individual voyages did not complete it.

Brazil received about 45 per cent of all captives and the Caribbean about a third; mainland North America took under 4 per cent, and its enslaved population grew mainly by natural increase, which was not the case further south. The traffic grew with sugar and peaked in the eighteenth century, when Portuguese, British and French ships carried the great majority. Ports from Lisbon and Nantes to Bristol and Liverpool grew on it, along with the credit, insurance and shipping businesses that financed it.

Its recorded consequences include depopulation, militarisation and political disruption in parts of West and West Central Africa, and in the Americas societies organised around racial slavery and the racial categories that accompanied it. Britain and the United States prohibited the trade in 1807 and 1808 and the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron tried to suppress it; an illegal traffic to Brazil and Cuba continued for decades, and the last known slave ship reached Cuba in 1867. Slavery itself outlasted the trade: it was abolished in the British empire in 1833, in the [United States](event:us-civil-war) in 1865, and in Brazil in 1888.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_slave_trade).

steps.name: The first direct crossings
steps.page:
Portuguese ships had carried enslaved Africans to Europe and the Atlantic islands since the 1440s. The first documented voyage direct from Africa to the Americas sailed in 1526, and a licensed traffic to the Spanish Caribbean followed.

Volumes were small by later standards, a few thousand a year, and much of the labour in early Spanish America was still Indigenous, under the *encomienda*.

steps.name: Sugar and the Brazilian trade
steps.page:
Sugar planting in north-eastern Brazil turned the trade into a system. Sugar is capital-intensive and labour-intensive, and Portuguese planters replaced dying Indigenous labour with captives shipped from Angola and the Bight of Benin.

Brazil became the largest single destination and remained so for three centuries, taking about 45 per cent of all captives carried across the Atlantic.

steps.name: The Caribbean plantation boom
steps.page:
English and French colonists in Barbados, the Leewards and Saint-Domingue adopted sugar from the Dutch after 1640 and remade their islands as plantation economies within a generation. Small farms were bought out and the population became overwhelmingly enslaved and African.

Chartered companies, the Dutch WIC and the Royal African Company from 1672, organised the supply, and colonial slave codes written in these decades fixed the legal status of enslaved people as property.

steps.name: The eighteenth-century peak
steps.page:
More than half of all captives were carried in the eighteenth century, most of them by Portuguese, British and French ships. Liverpool overtook Bristol and London as Britain's leading slaving port, and Nantes led in France.

The traffic drew in whole coastal economies. African states such as Dahomey, Asante and Oyo grew powerful on the exchange of captives for firearms and textiles, while raiding and war reached ever further inland to supply it.

steps.name: Abolition of the trade
steps.page:
After twenty years of campaigning by Quakers, evangelicals and formerly enslaved writers such as Olaudah Equiano, and after the [Haitian Revolution](event:haitian-revolution), Parliament abolished the British slave trade in March 1807.

Denmark had prohibited it from 1803; the United States barred further imports from 1 January 1808, the earliest date its constitution allowed. Slavery itself was untouched in all three.

steps.name: Suppression and the last voyages
steps.page:
The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron patrolled for six decades, intercepted about 1,600 ships and freed some 150,000 people, most of them landed at Freetown. It was expensive, and it made the passage more lethal as captains packed ships to outrun cruisers.

An illegal traffic to Brazil and Cuba continued regardless: over three million people were carried between 1810 and 1860. Brazil suppressed its own trade in 1850, and the last known slave ship reached Cuba in 1867.

name: The Scientific Revolution
summary: Between the middle of the sixteenth century and the end of the seventeenth, European natural philosophy replaced inherited authority with mathematics, observation and controlled experiment. Copernicus's heliocentric astronomy of 1543 is the conventional beginning and Newton's *Principia* of 1687 the conventional end.
body:
What changed was less the stock of facts than the standard of proof. Aristotle had been the authority on motion and Galen on the body; by 1700 an argument was expected to answer to measurement, and to measurements that other people could repeat. Instruments mattered as much as ideas: the telescope, the microscope, the air pump, the pendulum clock and the barometer each showed something no unaided sense could reach.

Mathematics carried much of the change. [Kepler](event:kepler) found that planets move on ellipses, [Galileo](event:galileo) that falling bodies accelerate uniformly and that motion persists without a cause, and [Newton](event:newton) that a single inverse-square law accounts for both. Descartes supplied coordinate geometry and a picture of the world as matter in motion; Bacon supplied a programme of organised, cooperative, published inquiry. Anatomy and chemistry followed the same route from authority to demonstration.

Institutions followed the ideas: the Accademia del Cimento in Florence, the Royal Society in London from 1660, the Académie des Sciences in Paris from 1666, and with them the scientific journal; the *Philosophical Transactions* began in 1665. Publication, criticism and replication became the ordinary practice of the subject and remain so. The confidence the new physics gave to reasoning about nature ran directly into the [Enlightenment](event:enlightenment).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_Revolution).

steps.name: Copernicus places the Sun at the centre
Vesalius maps the human body
steps.page:
In the same year as Copernicus's book, Andreas Vesalius published *De humani corporis fabrica* at Basel, a description of human anatomy based on his own dissections, with plates by artists from Titian's workshop.

It corrected Galen in hundreds of particulars, most of them cases where Galen had dissected animals and assumed people were the same. Vesalius dissected in person and published his own findings rather than the received text.

steps.name: Tycho Brahe's observatory
steps.page:
Tycho Brahe built Uraniborg on the island of Hven with Danish royal funding and observed for twenty years with large graduated instruments and no telescope, reaching an accuracy of about one minute of arc.

His new star of 1572 and comet of 1577 showed that the heavens change and that comets pass through the crystalline spheres they were supposed to be bounded by. [Kepler](event:kepler) inherited the observations at Tycho's death in 1601.

steps.name: Galileo turns a telescope on the sky
Bacon and Descartes on method
steps.page:
Francis Bacon's *Novum Organum* (1620) argued that knowledge of nature must be built up from organised observation and experiment, by many hands, and set against the biases he called idols of the mind.

René Descartes's *Discourse on Method* (1637) went the other way, from systematic doubt to certainty and thence to a world of matter in motion governed by geometry; its appendix introduced coordinate geometry. The two books set out the century's competing accounts of method, inductive and deductive.

steps.name: The Royal Society and the new institutions
steps.page:
The Royal Society was founded in London in 1660 to witness and record experiments collectively, taking as its motto *nullius in verba*, on no one's word. The Académie des Sciences followed in Paris in 1666.

Its *Philosophical Transactions*, begun in 1665, is the oldest scientific journal still published, and it established the practices of dated priority, published method and review by readers who had not witnessed the work.

name: Copernicus places the Sun at the centre
summary: Nicolaus Copernicus's *De revolutionibus orbium coelestium*, published in 1543 as he lay dying, argued that the Earth turns on its axis and orbits the Sun. It displaced the Earth from the centre of the universe and set the agenda for the astronomy of the next century.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Copernicus was a canon at Frombork in Poland, trained in law and medicine, who worked at astronomy for decades without publishing. He had circulated a manuscript summary, the *Commentariolus*, around 1514; the full book appeared only at the urging of the young mathematician Rheticus, and it carried an unsigned preface by Andreas Osiander presenting the system as a calculating device rather than a claim about the world.

The model puts the Sun at the centre with the planets, Earth among them, in the order still taught, and explains naturally what Ptolemaic astronomy handled with added machinery: why Mercury and Venus never stray far from the Sun, and why the outer planets appear to reverse direction. It was not simpler to use. Copernicus kept perfectly circular orbits and so needed epicycles of his own, and his tables predicted no better than the ones they replaced.

The objections were serious rather than merely obstinate: a moving Earth should produce a visible shift in the fixed stars, and none could be measured until 1838. Acceptance took a century and the work of [Kepler](event:kepler), [Galileo](event:galileo) and [Newton](event:newton). The book was placed on the Index of Prohibited Books in 1616, pending correction.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolaus_Copernicus).

name: Isaac Newton
summary: English mathematician and physicist who set out the laws of motion and universal gravitation, and who invented the calculus independently of Leibniz.
body:
Newton was born at Woolsthorpe in Lincolnshire on Christmas Day 1642 by the calendar then used in England, which is 4 January 1643 by the one used now. He went up to Trinity College, Cambridge, and did much of his most original work in 1665–67, when plague closed the university and he returned home.

The *[Principia](item:newton)* of 1687 gave three laws of motion and a law of universal gravitation, and showed that the same mathematics governs a falling apple, the tides, comets and the orbits of the planets. It is the central text of the [Scientific Revolution](item:scientific-revolution). To carry out the work he developed what he called fluxions, the [calculus](item:calculus), which Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz reached independently and published first, provoking a long priority dispute.

He also wrote the *Opticks*, demonstrated that white light is a mixture of colours, built the first reflecting telescope, spent decades on alchemy and biblical chronology, sat in Parliament, and ran the Royal Mint, where he prosecuted counterfeiters. He was President of the Royal Society from 1703 until his death.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton).

name: Calculus
summary: The mathematics of change: differentiation, which measures rates, integration, which accumulates them, and the theorem that the two are inverse operations.
body:
Areas and tangents had been attacked for two thousand years, by Archimedes with exhaustion arguments and by Fermat, Cavalieri and Barrow with methods that worked case by case. What [Newton](item:isaac-newton) and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz supplied in the 1660s and 1670s was a general calculus: a notation and a set of rules that made the problems routine, and the fundamental theorem linking the two operations.

Newton developed his fluxions first and used them in the *[Principia](item:newton)*, though he presented the results there in classical geometry. Leibniz published first, and his notation, dx, dy and the integral sign, is the one still in use. The priority dispute between them, and between their national followers, lasted decades.

The foundations were shaky for a century and a half: infinitesimals were quantities that had to be non-zero and then zero, an objection Bishop Berkeley put memorably. Cauchy and Weierstrass replaced them with limits in the nineteenth century. By then the calculus had become the standard language of physics and engineering, and the basis of the differential equations used to describe continuous processes.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculus).

name: The Enlightenment
summary: The Enlightenment was an intellectual movement of the long eighteenth century which held that reason, evidence and free criticism should decide any claim, whether about nature, religion or government. It ran from roughly the 1680s to the end of the century, centred on France, Britain, Scotland and the German states.
body:
Its confidence came from the [new science](event:scientific-revolution): if the heavens obeyed laws that a person could work out, so might society. Locke argued that knowledge comes from experience and that government rests on consent and may be dissolved; [Montesquieu](event:montesquieu-spirit) analysed how power might be divided so that it checks itself; [Voltaire](event:voltaire-enlightenment) attacked judicial cruelty, censorship and clerical privilege; [Hume](event:hume-philosophy) pressed empiricism to sceptical conclusions; [Rousseau](event:rousseau-social) dissented from much of it, holding that civilisation corrupts; [Adam Smith](event:wealth-of-nations) described a commercial society ordered without anyone directing it; Kant answered the question "what is enlightenment?" with the motto *sapere aude*, dare to know.

It was carried by print and by sociability rather than by universities: the [*Encyclopédie*](event:diderot-encyclopedia), pamphlets, cheap pirated reprints, coffee houses, Parisian salons run by women, provincial academies and masonic lodges. Much of it was printed abroad or clandestinely to evade the censors. Beccaria's argument against torture and the death penalty, and the campaign against the [slave trade](event:slave-trade), show what it produced in practice.

Its politics were not uniform: some looked to reforming monarchs ([enlightened absolutism](event:enlightened-despotism)), others to representative government. Its language of natural rights and popular sovereignty passed into the [American](event:american-revolution) and [French](event:french-revolution) revolutions. Critics from the Romantics onward charged it with a thin view of tradition, feeling and community, and with a universalism that in practice excluded women, the poor and the colonised.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment).

name: Newton's Principia
summary: Isaac Newton's *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica*, published in 1687, set out three laws of motion and a law of universal gravitation. A single set of principles accounted for falling bodies, the tides, the paths of comets and the orbits of the planets.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). The book was written in about eighteen months after Edmond Halley asked [Newton](item:isaac-newton) what curve a planet would follow under an inverse-square attraction and was told, from memory, an ellipse; Newton had worked it out years earlier and mislaid the proof. Halley paid for the printing himself.

The first law says a body keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless a force acts on it; the second relates force to change of motion; the third pairs every action with an equal and opposite reaction. Gravitation is universal: every mass attracts every other in proportion to the product of the masses and inversely as the square of the distance between them. From these Newton derived [Kepler's laws](event:kepler), explained the tides by the pull of Moon and Sun, showed why the Earth bulges at the equator, and made comets predictable, a prediction Halley's comet kept in 1758.

The argument is presented in classical geometry rather than in the [calculus](item:calculus) Newton had invented and used, which is one reason the book is so hard. He declined to say what gravity *is*, writing *hypotheses non fingo*, I feign no hypotheses, and gave only the law by which it acts, an omission Continental followers of Descartes attacked for decades as a return to occult qualities. The *Principia* set the standard the sciences aimed at for two hundred years, until [relativity](event:relativity) showed the limits of its account of gravity without displacing it as a working theory.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophiæ_Naturalis_Principia_Mathematica).

name: Industrial Revolution
summary: From about 1760 Britain began making goods with machines driven by water and then by coal-fired steam, in factories rather than in households. Output per worker rose faster than population for the first time in history, and the pattern spread to western Europe, North America and eventually the world.
body:
Textiles came first, because spinning was the bottleneck: [the jenny, the water frame and the mule](event:spinning-jenny) multiplied what one worker could produce, and the work moved to where the power was. [Watt's engine](event:watt-engine), with its separate condenser and later its rotary drive, freed factories from riverbanks. Coke smelting and Cort's puddling process made cheap wrought iron; canals and then [railways](event:railways) carried coal, iron and cloth at a fraction of the old cost. Britain had the coal, the shipping, the colonial markets, the patent law and the capital, and historians still argue about which of those mattered most.

The social consequences arrived faster than any means of handling them. Manchester's population multiplied several times over in fifty years, into housing without drains or clean water, and life expectancy in the industrial towns was lower than in the countryside they drew on. Work was disciplined by the clock and the machine rather than by daylight and season. Children worked in mills and mines until the Factory Acts began restricting it from 1833. Handloom weavers were ruined; the Luddites broke frames in 1811–13; trade unions, the Chartist movement and a new vocabulary of class all came out of the same decades.

Sustained growth in output per head, energy use, urbanisation and population all begin their steep rise here, and so does the atmospheric carbon dioxide behind [modern climate change](event:global-warming).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution).

steps.name: Cromford and the factory system
steps.page:
Richard Arkwright's mill at Cromford, opened in 1771, ran water-powered frames day and night with a workforce of several hundred, many of them children, housed in a village built for them.

The organisation mattered as much as the machine: fixed hours, shifts, supervision and a discipline of the clock that had no precedent in the domestic workshops it replaced.

steps.name: Cheap iron: coke, puddling and the first iron bridge
steps.page:
Abraham Darby's family had smelted iron with coke rather than charcoal at Coalbrookdale since 1709, breaking the dependence on woodland. In 1779 the third Darby cast the world's first iron bridge over the Severn there.

Henry Cort's puddling and rolling process, patented in 1783–84, made wrought iron from pig iron with coal rather than charcoal and at many times the rate. Cheap iron made machines, rails, boilers and iron ships possible.

steps.name: Steam-powered cotton and the mule
steps.page:
