The first Boulton and Watt rotative engine drove a cotton mill at Papplewick in 1785, and steam quickly displaced water in the Lancashire trade because a mill could then be built where the labour and the canal were.

Crompton's mule was scaled up and fitted with steam drive; Cartwright's power loom, patented in 1785, took another two decades to become practical. British raw cotton consumption rose more than tenfold in twenty years.

steps.name: The factory town and the first Factory Acts
steps.page:
By the 1830s the consequences were being counted: cholera in 1832, Chadwick's sanitary inquiry, and evidence to parliamentary commissions about children working twelve-hour days in mills and hauling in mines.

The Factory Act of 1833 limited children's hours in textile mills and, for the first time, appointed inspectors to enforce it. The Mines Act of 1842 followed. Neither went far, and both established that the state would regulate what went on inside a private factory.

name: Napoleon Bonaparte
summary: French general who made himself emperor, dominated Europe for a decade, and left behind a legal code still in use across much of the world.
body:
Born on Corsica a year after France annexed it, Napoleon was trained at French military schools and made his name in the artillery during [the Revolution](item:french-revolution). Command in Italy and an expedition to Egypt built his reputation; in 1799 he [seized power](item:napoleon-coup) in a coup, and in 1804 crowned himself emperor.

As a commander he moved armies faster than his opponents could react and concentrated force at the decisive point; [Austerlitz](item:austerlitz) in 1805 is the usual textbook example. [The wars](item:napoleonic-wars) that carry his name put most of Europe under French control or influence, but Britain held the sea after [Trafalgar](item:trafalgar), Spain became an unwinnable guerrilla war, and [the invasion of Russia](item:russia-1812) in 1812 destroyed the Grande Armée. He abdicated in 1814, returned for a hundred days, and was beaten at [Waterloo](item:waterloo).

He died in British custody on Saint Helena. The Napoleonic Code, a centralised administration, the metric system and conscription outlasted him, and the nationalism his campaigns provoked ran through European politics for a century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon).

name: American Revolution
summary: Thirteen British colonies in North America went to war with Britain in 1775, declared independence in 1776 and won recognition of it in 1783. The new United States then wrote a federal constitution, and was the first modern republic founded on a written statement of natural rights.
body:
The quarrel followed the [Seven Years' War](event:seven-years-war), when Parliament tried to make the colonies pay a share of imperial defence through the Stamp Act, the Townshend duties and the tea tax. Colonists objected that they were being taxed by a body in which they were not represented, and that their own assemblies had long held that power. Boycotts, riots and Britain's coercive response to the destruction of tea in Boston harbour in 1773 hardened both sides, and shooting began at Lexington and Concord in April 1775.

Britain's problem was distance and the absence of a decisive target. Washington's Continental Army had to be kept in being rather than made to win, and it survived Long Island, the loss of New York and Philadelphia and the winter at Valley Forge. Saratoga in 1777 brought France into the war in 1778, followed by Spain and the Dutch Republic, turning a colonial rebellion into a global one that stretched British forces from Gibraltar to India. A French fleet closed the Chesapeake and made [Yorktown](event:yorktown) a surrender rather than a siege that could be relieved.

Perhaps a fifth of the population stayed loyal to the Crown, and some 60,000 left, most for Canada. Native nations, most of which had sided with Britain as the power more likely to restrain settlement, lost their protector in the peace. Slavery survived the language of the [Declaration](event:declaration-independence): northern states began abolishing it, southern states did not, and the question was deferred into the [Constitution](event:us-constitution) and eventually into a civil war. The revolution's example, and the debt France ran up paying for it, contributed to the [French Revolution](event:french-revolution) six years later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution).

steps.name: Lexington and Concord
steps.page:
British regulars marched out of Boston on the night of 18 April 1775 to seize militia stores at Concord. Riders including Paul Revere raised the countryside ahead of them.

Shots were exchanged on Lexington green at dawn and again at Concord bridge, and the column was fired on from behind walls all the way back to Boston, losing some 270 men. Within weeks a militia army had besieged the city.

steps.name: Saratoga and the French alliance
steps.page:
A British army under Burgoyne moving south from Canada was fought to a standstill at Freeman's Farm and Bemis Heights and surrendered nearly 6,000 men at Saratoga on 17 October 1777.

It was the first surrender of a British army in the war, and it convinced France that the Americans could win. The treaties of alliance and commerce were signed in Paris on 6 February 1778, turning a colonial rebellion into a European war.

steps.name: The war moves south
steps.page:
Unable to force a decision in the north, Britain turned to the southern colonies, expecting loyalist support. Savannah fell in December 1778 and Charleston in May 1780, with the capture of a whole American army.

What followed was a partisan war of raids and reprisals. Greene's campaign traded ground for time, and Cornwallis, having won at Guilford Court House in March 1781 at ruinous cost, marched into Virginia with an army worn thin.

steps.name: The Treaty of Paris
steps.page:
Negotiations opened in Paris in 1782, with Franklin, Adams and Jay dealing separately with Britain despite the French alliance and getting better terms for it.

The treaty signed on 3 September 1783 recognised the United States as independent and granted a western boundary at the Mississippi, more than the fighting had won, over the heads of the Native nations who had fought as British allies. Britain settled separately with France and Spain the same day.

name: French Revolution
summary: The French Revolution began in 1789 with a fiscal crisis that became the collapse of the old regime. In ten years France abolished feudal privilege and the monarchy, executed its king, fought most of Europe, killed thousands of its own citizens in the Terror, and ended under a general who made himself ruler.
body:
The crown was bankrupt, partly from the [American war](event:american-revolution), and could not raise taxes without the consent of the privileged orders. The Estates-General met in May 1789 for the first time since 1614; the third estate declared itself a National Assembly, and the [storming of the Bastille](event:bastille) in July, together with a rural panic that summer, forced the abolition of feudal dues and the [Declaration of the Rights of Man](event:rights-of-man).

The constitutional monarchy of 1791 failed. The king's attempted flight destroyed what trust in him remained; war with Austria and Prussia from April 1792 turned every political question into a question of treason; and the monarchy fell in August. Louis XVI was executed in January 1793. Facing invasion, civil war in the Vendée and bread riots, the Convention delegated emergency power to the Committee of Public Safety, and the [Terror](event:terror) that followed executed some 17,000 people by sentence and killed many more in the provinces and in prison. Robespierre fell in July 1794.

The Directory that governed from 1795 balanced between royalists and Jacobins, annulled elections it disliked, and leaned increasingly on an army that was winning in Italy and Germany. In November 1799 [Bonaparte](item:napoleon-bonaparte) [overthrew it](event:napoleon-coup). What the revolution left behind was legal equality, the end of seigneurial and clerical privilege, the metric system, a civil code, conscription and the nation in arms, along with a political vocabulary of left and right, citizen, terror, reaction and ideology that has been in use since.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution).

steps.name: The Estates-General and the National Assembly
steps.page:
The Estates-General met at Versailles on 5 May 1789 for the first time since 1614, to solve a fiscal crisis nobody else could. It deadlocked at once over whether the three orders should vote separately, which would let clergy and nobility outvote everyone else.

On 17 June the third estate declared itself a National Assembly with the right to speak for the nation. Locked out of its hall three days later, it gathered in an indoor tennis court and swore not to disperse until France had a constitution.

steps.name: Declaration of the Rights of Man
The flight to Varennes
steps.page:
The royal family slipped out of the Tuileries on the night of 20 June 1791 in a conspicuous coach, heading for loyal troops on the eastern frontier, and were recognised and stopped at Varennes.

Louis had left behind a letter denouncing everything he had agreed to. Brought back through silent crowds, he was suspended and then restored, and signed the constitution in September. Confidence in the king was not restored with him.

steps.name: War, the fall of the monarchy and the republic
steps.page:
France declared war on Austria in April 1792 and lost the opening campaign. A manifesto threatening Paris with destruction if the king were harmed produced the opposite: on 10 August a crowd and the Paris sections stormed the Tuileries and the monarchy fell.

Prisoners were massacred in September amid panic about invasion; the army held at Valmy on 20 September; the Convention proclaimed a republic the next day. Louis was tried by it as an ordinary citizen and guillotined on 21 January 1793.

steps.name: Thermidor and the Directory
steps.page:
With Robespierre dead the emergency machinery was dismantled, price controls went, and a harsh winter and inflation fell on the poor of Paris, whose risings were now put down by the army.

The constitution of 1795 set up a five-man Directory and two councils. It survived by annulling elections that went against it, from either side, and depended increasingly on generals, most conspicuously on the young commander of the army of Italy.

name: Napoleonic Wars
summary: France under Napoleon fought most of Europe for twelve years and briefly dominated the continent.
body:
Part of [French Revolution](event:french-revolution). The Napoleonic Wars were a series of conflicts fought between 1803 and 1815 by [Napoleon's](item:napoleon-bonaparte) France and a shifting set of coalitions led by Britain, Austria, Prussia and Russia. France won almost every campaign on land for a decade and at its height controlled or dominated most of continental Europe. It was worn down by the war in Spain, by the destruction of the Grande Armée in Russia and by the coalition of 1813 to 1815.

The wars grew out of the [French Revolution](event:french-revolution) and the revolutionary wars that preceded them, and resumed after the short-lived Peace of Amiens broke down in May 1803. France's advantage on land rested on large conscript armies, a corps system that could march and fight separately, and a commander willing to take risks for a decisive battle. Britain's advantage was money and command of the sea.

Roughly three to six million people died, soldiers and civilians together. The wars carried the Napoleonic Code, the metric system, conscription and the administrative state across Europe, dissolved the Holy Roman Empire, and contributed to national movements in Germany, Italy and Spain. The Congress of Vienna settlement of 1814–15 restored monarchies but also built a balance of power that kept the great states from a general European war until [1914](event:ww1). Spain's collapse under French occupation also loosened its grip on the Americas, where the [independence wars](event:latam-independence) began in 1810.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars).

steps.name: The rupture of Amiens
steps.page:
The Peace of Amiens, signed in 1802, was the only interval of general peace between France and Britain in twenty-two years, and it lasted fourteen months. Britain refused to evacuate Malta as agreed, France continued to expand its influence in Italy, Switzerland and the Low Countries, and Britain declared war on 18 May 1803.

Napoleon massed an army of invasion at Boulogne and gathered the barges to carry it, which required command of the Channel for long enough to cross.

steps.name: Jena and Auerstedt
steps.page:
Prussia mobilised against France in 1806 and was destroyed in a fortnight. Two battles fought on the same day, 14 October, at Jena and at Auerstedt, broke the Prussian army; Berlin was occupied a fortnight later.

Napoleon then fought the Russians to a standstill in Poland and East Prussia through the winter and beat them at Friedland in June 1807. The treaties of Tilsit that followed left France dominant from the Rhine to the Niemen and brought Russia into the Continental System, the blockade of British trade.

steps.name: The Peninsular War
steps.page:
French troops occupied Spain in 1808 and Napoleon put his brother Joseph on its throne. The rising in Madrid on 2 May and the surrender of a French corps at Bailén in July showed that a Spanish population in arms could not be dealt with as an army could.

Six years of siege, battle and guerrilla warfare followed, with a British army under Wellesley (later the Duke of Wellington) holding Portugal and advancing from it. Napoleon called it his Spanish ulcer; it consumed several hundred thousand French troops.

steps.name: Leipzig
steps.page:
With the Grande Armée destroyed in Russia, Prussia and then Austria changed sides. Napoleon raised a new army of conscripts and won at Lützen and Bautzen, but could not force a peace.

Half a million men fought at Leipzig over four days in October 1813, the largest battle in Europe before 1914. The French were beaten and driven back across the Rhine, and the Confederation of the Rhine collapsed with them.

steps.name: The first abdication
steps.page:
The coalition invaded France from the east while Wellington crossed the Pyrenees from Spain. Napoleon manoeuvred skilfully with a much smaller army through the winter of 1814, but Paris surrendered on 31 March and his marshals refused to march on it.

He abdicated on 6 April 1814 and was given the island of Elba and the title of emperor of it. The Bourbons were restored, and the powers met at Vienna to settle the map of Europe.

steps.name: The peace of 1815
steps.page:
The Congress of Vienna closed its Final Act nine days before Waterloo. It restored the Bourbons, enlarged the Netherlands and Prussia as barriers against France, confirmed the end of the Holy Roman Empire, and set up a balance in which no single power could dominate the continent.

The second Treaty of Paris of 20 November 1815 imposed an indemnity and an army of occupation on France but left its 1790 borders intact. Napoleon was sent to St Helena. The settlement held the great powers back from a general European war until [1914](item:ww1).

name: Charles Darwin
summary: English naturalist who established that species descend with modification from common ancestors, and proposed natural selection as the mechanism.
body:
Charles Darwin (1809–1882) was an English naturalist who showed that living species are descended with modification from common ancestors, and who proposed [natural selection](item:natural-selection) as the process that shapes them. [*On the Origin of Species*](item:origin-species), published in 1859, set out the evidence and the argument together. It is the foundation of modern biology.

Darwin abandoned medicine at Edinburgh and read for the clergy at Cambridge before sailing as naturalist on HMS *Beagle* in 1831. The five-year voyage took him along the coasts of South America and to the Galápagos, and the fossils, geology and island species he collected there occupied him for the rest of his life.

He worked out the principle of natural selection by 1838 but published nothing for twenty years, spending them instead on barnacles, orchids and correspondence. In 1858 Alfred Russel Wallace sent him an essay reaching the same conclusion; their work was read jointly to the Linnean Society, and the *Origin* followed the next year.

Later books extended the argument to human ancestry, to sexual selection and to the expression of emotion. Darwin lived quietly at Down House in Kent, in poor health, and is buried in Westminster Abbey. Descent with modification is now the organising principle of biology, and its union with genetics after the [structure of DNA](item:dna-structure) was established has left the core of his argument intact.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Darwin).

name: Abraham Lincoln
summary: Sixteenth president of the United States, who led the Union through the Civil War and made the abolition of slavery its object.
body:
Abraham Lincoln (1809–1865) was the sixteenth president of the United States. He held the Union together through the [Civil War](item:us-civil-war), made the destruction of slavery one of its objects, and was assassinated five days after the Confederate surrender. He is generally ranked among the country's most consequential presidents.

Lincoln was born in a Kentucky log cabin, had perhaps a year of formal schooling, and taught himself law in Illinois. A Whig legislator and one-term congressman, he returned to politics over the extension of slavery into the territories, lost a Senate race to Stephen Douglas in 1858 after a celebrated series of debates, and was elected president in 1860 on the new Republican ticket.

Seven states seceded before he took office and war began within six weeks. He held the border states, blockaded the South, and cycled through commanders until he found Grant. The [Emancipation Proclamation](item:emancipation) of 1863 turned the war for the Union into a war against slavery and opened the army to black soldiers; his address at [Gettysburg](item:gettysburg) that November restated the war as a test of whether government by consent could survive.

Re-elected in 1864, he pressed the Thirteenth Amendment through Congress and argued for a lenient peace. Five days after Lee's surrender he was [shot at Ford's Theatre](item:lincoln-assassination), the first American president to be assassinated.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln).

name: Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species
summary: Darwin set out the theory that species descend with modification from common ancestors through natural selection.
body:
*On the Origin of Species* was published in London on 24 November 1859. In it [Charles Darwin](item:charles-darwin) argued that species are not fixed but descend with modification from common ancestors, and that the process producing them is [natural selection](item:natural-selection): heritable variation, more offspring than can survive, and the differential survival that follows. The first printing of 1,250 copies sold out at once.

Darwin had held the argument back for twenty years and published only when Alfred Russel Wallace sent him an essay from the Malay Archipelago reaching the same conclusion. The book itself is a long accumulation of evidence from domestic breeding, the fossil record, geographical distribution, embryology and rudimentary organs, presented as one argument rather than as a set of proofs, and it deals openly with the objections Darwin could not answer.

The weakest point was heredity: Darwin had no mechanism for how variation was passed on or preserved, and blending inheritance would have destroyed it. That gap closed only when Mendelian genetics was joined to selection in the modern synthesis of the 1930s and 1940s, and again with the [structure of DNA](event:dna-structure). Common descent was accepted by biologists within a decade or two; natural selection as the main mechanism took much longer. The book is the founding work of evolutionary biology. Opposition to it continued, including at the [Scopes trial](event:scopes-trial) in 1925.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Origin_of_Species).

name: Evolution by natural selection
summary: The explanation of adaptation without design: heritable variation plus differential survival and reproduction, repeated over generations.
body:
Natural selection is the process that produces adaptation without a designer. Where organisms vary, where some of that variation is inherited, and where more offspring are produced than can survive, the variants that leave more descendants become more common. Repeated over many generations, this shapes populations in ways that look designed.

The argument has three premises and one conclusion, and each premise is an observation rather than an assumption. [Darwin](item:charles-darwin) and Alfred Russel Wallace arrived at it independently and published jointly in 1858; [*On the Origin of Species*](item:origin-species) set out the evidence the following year.

Its weakest point was heredity, for which Darwin had no mechanism, and it was resolved only when Mendelian genetics was combined with selection in the modern synthesis of the 1930s and 40s, and again by the [structure of DNA](item:dna-structure) and the reading of [whole genomes](item:human-genome).

Natural selection is not the only evolutionary process: drift, migration and mutation all change populations, and much molecular change is effectively neutral. It is, however, the only known process that produces adaptation, and it applies wherever there is heritable variation in reproductive success, including bacteria acquiring antibiotic resistance and viruses evolving during an epidemic.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_selection).

name: American Civil War
summary: Eleven southern states seceded to preserve slavery; four years of war ended slavery and cost some 700,000 lives.
body:
The American Civil War was fought from April 1861 to the spring of 1865 between the United States (the Union) and the Confederate States, eleven southern states that had seceded after the election of [Abraham Lincoln](item:abraham-lincoln). The Confederacy was defeated, secession was ended, and slavery was abolished throughout the country. About 700,000 soldiers died, more Americans than in any other war.

Slavery was the cause. The Confederate states seceded to protect an institution that held four million people, and said so in their declarations of secession; the immediate trigger was the election of a president committed to keeping slavery out of the western territories. Lincoln's war aim at the start was the restoration of the Union rather than abolition, which was what held the slaveholding border states in it.

The North had four times the free population, most of the industry, most of the railways and a navy. The South had to defend rather than conquer, had better field commanders in the east for the first two years, and hoped that European powers dependent on its cotton would intervene. Union strategy settled into blockade of the coast, control of the Mississippi to split the Confederacy in two, and pressure on the Confederate armies in Virginia and Tennessee at once.

The [Emancipation Proclamation](event:emancipation) of 1863 turned the war into a war against slavery, made European recognition of the Confederacy politically impossible, and brought some 180,000 black soldiers and sailors into Union service. In 1864 Grant took command in the east and fought Lee continuously rather than in separate campaigns, while Sherman took Atlanta and marched to the sea, destroying the resources the Confederate armies lived on.

Lee surrendered at Appomattox on 9 April 1865 and the remaining Confederate forces gave up over the following weeks. Lincoln was [assassinated](event:lincoln-assassination) five days after Appomattox. The Thirteenth, Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments abolished slavery and wrote citizenship and voting rights into the constitution; the Reconstruction that was to enforce them was abandoned by 1877, and the South imposed segregation and disenfranchisement that lasted until the [civil rights movement](event:civil-rights).

The war's course is followed in the steps below.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War).

steps.name: Fort Sumter
steps.page:
Confederate batteries opened fire on the Federal garrison of Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour on 12 April 1861, after Lincoln announced that he would resupply it. The fort surrendered the next day; nobody was killed in the bombardment.

Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers to suppress the rebellion, and four more states (Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee and North Carolina) seceded rather than furnish troops against their neighbours.

steps.name: First Bull Run
steps.page:
The first large battle was fought on 21 July 1861 beside a stream called Bull Run, thirty miles from Washington, between armies of ninety-day volunteers watched by spectators who had driven out from the capital.

The Union attack broke up in confusion and the retreat became a rout. It ended the expectation on both sides that the war would be settled in a single campaign, and the Union began raising and training armies for a long one.

steps.name: Antietam
steps.page:
Lee invaded Maryland in September 1862 and was met at Antietam Creek on the 17th. Around 22,000 men were killed, wounded or missing in a single day, the bloodiest day in American history.

The battle was tactically inconclusive but Lee withdrew into Virginia, which was enough of a victory for Lincoln to announce the preliminary [Emancipation Proclamation](item:emancipation) five days later, and enough to end any prospect of British or French recognition of the Confederacy.

steps.name: Vicksburg
steps.page:
Vicksburg on its bluff was the last Confederate stronghold on the Mississippi. Grant crossed the river below it, marched inland away from his supply line, beat the forces in his way and then besieged the city from the land side for six weeks.

The garrison of about 30,000 surrendered on 4 July 1863, the day after [Gettysburg](item:gettysburg). The Union now held the river along its whole length, and the Confederacy was cut in two.

steps.name: Sherman's March to the Sea
steps.page:
After taking Atlanta in September 1864, a victory that helped re-elect Lincoln in November, Sherman cut loose from his supply line and marched 60,000 men across Georgia to Savannah, which he reached three days before Christmas.

His army lived off the country and destroyed railways, mills, cotton and food stores as it went. The march was directed at the will and the means to continue the war rather than at an opposing army, and Sherman turned north into the Carolinas to repeat it.

steps.name: Appomattox
steps.page:
Grant's Overland Campaign of 1864 cost enormous casualties and pinned Lee at Petersburg through a nine-month siege. When the line broke on 2 April 1865 Richmond was abandoned and burned, and Lee's army marched west with the Union cavalry ahead of it.

Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia at Appomattox Court House on 9 April. The terms let his men go home with their horses, and the pattern was followed by the surrenders that ended the war elsewhere over the following seven weeks.

name: Mohandas Gandhi
summary: Leader of the Indian independence movement, who made non-violent mass civil disobedience an instrument of political change.
body:
Mohandas Gandhi (1869–1948) led the Indian independence movement and made organised non-violent civil disobedience an instrument of mass politics. He turned the Indian National Congress into a movement with a popular base, and his methods were studied and copied by campaigns for civil rights and against colonial rule across the world.

Gandhi trained as a barrister in London and spent twenty years in South Africa, where discrimination against Indian residents led him to develop *satyagraha*, a form of non-violent resistance in which participants openly refuse to comply with a law and accept the penalty for it.

Returning to India in 1915, he organised peasants and mill workers, launched non-cooperation with [British rule](item:british-raj), and in 1930 walked 385 kilometres to the sea to make salt in defiance of the government monopoly; the [Salt March](item:salt-march) drew tens of thousands into civil disobedience. The [Quit India](item:quit-india) movement of 1942 brought him and most of the Congress leadership to prison.

He campaigned against untouchability and for Hindu-Muslim unity, and opposed [the partition](item:partition) that accompanied [independence](item:indian-independence) in 1947. He was shot in Delhi in January 1948 by a Hindu nationalist who thought him too conciliatory towards Muslims. His methods were studied closely by later movements, among them the [American civil rights campaign](item:civil-rights).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi).

name: Albert Einstein
summary: Theoretical physicist whose work on relativity, light quanta and statistical mechanics changed the physics of space, time, matter and energy.
body:
Albert Einstein (1879–1955) was a theoretical physicist whose work reorganised the physics of space, time, matter and energy. [Special relativity](item:relativity) abandoned absolute time, general relativity replaced gravitational force with the curvature of spacetime, and his paper on light quanta was one of the founding documents of quantum theory. He is widely regarded as one of the most influential scientists of the twentieth century.

Einstein was born at Ulm and educated in Munich, Aarau and Zurich. Unable to find an academic post, he took work at the Swiss patent office in Bern, and in 1905, his *annus mirabilis*, published four papers in a single year: on the photoelectric effect, on Brownian motion, on the electrodynamics of moving bodies, and on the equivalence of mass and energy.

Ten years later general relativity recast gravity as geometry; the bending of starlight measured during the 1919 eclipse made him famous outside physics. The theory's later predictions include black holes and [gravitational waves](item:gravitational-waves), detected a century after he wrote it down. See also the article on [relativity](item:theory-of-relativity).

He received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for the photoelectric effect rather than for relativity. A Jewish pacifist, he left Germany when [Hitler took power](item:hitler-chancellor) and settled at Princeton, where he spent his last two decades on an unsuccessful search for a unified field theory and in public argument against militarism and racial segregation. In 1939 he signed a letter to President Roosevelt warning that [nuclear fission](item:nuclear-fission) might make a bomb possible. He later described the letter as his one great mistake.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Einstein).

name: Modern global warming
summary: Greenhouse gases released since the Industrial Revolution have warmed the planet by about 1.3 °C, and the rate is increasing.
body:
Modern global warming is the rise in the earth's surface temperature caused by greenhouse gases released by human activity, chiefly carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels. The global average is now about 1.3 °C above the late-nineteenth-century baseline, and the warming is continuing.

The physics has been understood for a long time. Fourier described the atmosphere's heat-trapping effect in the 1820s, Tyndall measured which gases do it in the 1850s, and Arrhenius calculated in 1896 roughly how much warming a doubling of carbon dioxide would produce. Continuous measurement of atmospheric CO2 began at Mauna Loa in 1958 and has risen every year since, from about 280 parts per million before the [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution) to over 420 today.

The observed consequences include the loss of mass from ice sheets and mountain glaciers, sea level rise of over 20 centimetres since 1900 and accelerating, ocean acidification, shifts in the ranges of species, and a measurable increase in the frequency and intensity of extreme heat. Attribution studies now link individual heatwaves and floods to the warming with quantified confidence.

The international response runs through the framework convention of 1992, the [Kyoto Protocol](event:kyoto-protocol) and the [Paris Agreement](event:paris-agreement) of 2015, which aims to hold warming well below 2 °C. Emissions have not yet peaked. The closest geological analogue for a rapid carbon release is the [PETM](event:petm), 56 million years ago, which was far slower.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_warming).

name: Einstein's theory of relativity
summary: Einstein's relativity described space and time as aspects of a single flexible geometry, and mass as a form of energy.
body:
Between 1905 and 1915 [Albert Einstein](item:albert-einstein) published the two theories of relativity. Special relativity made the speed of light the same for every observer and abandoned absolute time; general relativity replaced the force of gravity with the curvature of spacetime produced by mass and energy. Together they are the framework in which large-scale physics is done.

Special relativity resolved a contradiction between Newtonian mechanics, in which velocities simply add, and Maxwell's electromagnetism, which gives light a fixed speed. Einstein's resolution was to keep the fixed speed and give up simultaneity: moving clocks run slow, moving lengths contract, and mass and energy are the same quantity in different units. General relativity, ten years later, explained the anomalous precession of Mercury's orbit and predicted that starlight passing the sun would be deflected, which was measured during the eclipse of 1919 and made Einstein famous outside physics.

The effects are not confined to extreme conditions. Satellite navigation must correct for both the speed of its clocks and the weaker gravity at orbital height. Black holes, the expanding universe and [gravitational waves](event:gravitational-waves) all follow from general relativity, and the last of these was detected a century after it was written down. See the article on [relativity](item:theory-of-relativity) for the theory itself.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theory_of_relativity).

name: Relativity
summary: The theory that space and time form a single flexible geometry, that the speed of light is the same for every observer, and that gravity is the curvature of that geometry.
body:
Relativity is the theory that space and time form a single flexible geometry, that light travels at the same speed for every observer, and that gravity is the curvature of that geometry rather than a force acting across it. It is the framework for physics at large scales, from satellite navigation to cosmology.

Special relativity, published by [Einstein](item:albert-einstein) in 1905, begins from two propositions: the laws of physics are the same for all observers in uniform motion, and light travels at the same speed for all of them. Absolute simultaneity, absolute length and absolute time do not survive. Moving clocks run slow, moving lengths contract, and mass and energy turn out to be the same quantity in different units.

General relativity followed in 1915. Gravity is not a force acting across space but the curvature of spacetime produced by mass and energy; bodies in free fall follow the straightest available paths through it. The theory predicted the precession of Mercury's orbit, the bending of starlight confirmed in 1919, and the slowing of clocks in a gravitational field that satellite navigation must correct for.

Its stranger predictions took a century to confirm: black holes, the expansion of the universe, and [gravitational waves](item:gravitational-waves), first detected in 2015. Relativity has so far agreed with every experiment and has not been reconciled with quantum mechanics. See also the entry on [Einstein's theory of relativity](item:relativity).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theory_of_relativity).

name: World War I
summary: Four years of industrial-scale war killed some 20 million people and destroyed four empires.
body:
World War I was fought from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918 between the Allies (chiefly France, Russia, Britain and their empires, with Italy from 1915 and the United States from 1917) and the Central Powers of Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria. Estimates of the dead run from 15 to 22 million, soldiers and civilians together. The Central Powers were defeated, and four empires (German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman) did not survive the war.

The immediate cause was the [assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand](event:sarajevo) in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914, which Austria-Hungary used to force a reckoning with Serbia. Behind it stood a system of alliances, a naval and military arms race, and a Balkan question the powers had already brought themselves to the edge over in [1908](event:bosnian-crisis). Within five weeks of the murder, mobilisation timetables and treaty obligations had drawn in every great power in Europe.

Germany's opening plan was to knock France out quickly by marching through Belgium and then turn east. It failed at the Marne, and by the end of 1914 the Western Front was a continuous line of trenches from the Channel to the Swiss border. Artillery, machine guns, barbed wire and railways gave the defender an advantage that neither side could break for three years; the offensives mounted to break it (Verdun, the Somme, Passchendaele) cost hundreds of thousands of casualties for a few kilometres. The war was fought as well in Russia and Galicia, in the Alps, at Gallipoli, in Mesopotamia and Palestine, in Africa, and at sea, where the British blockade and the German submarine campaign attacked each other's food and trade.

It was also the first war fought by whole societies: conscription, war economies, rationing, censorship and propaganda, and women in factories and offices in numbers there had been no precedent for. The strain broke Russia first, in [revolution](event:russian-revolution) in 1917, and Germany last, in mutiny and revolution in the autumn of 1918.

The armistice of 11 November 1918 was followed by the [Treaty of Versailles](event:versailles) and the settlements with the other defeated states. They redrew central Europe into new national states, distributed the Ottoman provinces of the Middle East as mandates, and imposed reparations and war guilt on Germany. The peace left grievances that were still live twenty years later, and the mobilised armies helped carry the [influenza pandemic](event:spanish-flu) around the world as they went home.

The steps below follow the war from the July Crisis to the armistice.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I).

steps.name: The July Crisis
steps.page:
The heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne was [shot at Sarajevo](item:sarajevo) on 28 June 1914. Vienna held Serbia responsible, obtained Germany's promise of support, and on 23 July sent an ultimatum written to be refused; Serbia accepted almost all of it, and Austria-Hungary declared war on 28 July.

Russia mobilised in Serbia's support. Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August, and invaded Belgium on 4 August to turn the French frontier defences; Britain, a guarantor of Belgian neutrality, declared war the same evening. Five of Europe's six great powers were at war within a week.

steps.name: The Marne
steps.page:
The German advance came within about 50 km of Paris before a gap opened between its two right-flank armies. French and British forces counter-attacked into it between 5 and 12 September 1914 and forced a German withdrawal to the Aisne.

The battle ended any prospect of a short war in the west. Both sides then extended their lines northwards to the sea, and by November the front was a continuous entrenched line from Nieuwpoort to the Swiss frontier that moved very little for the next three years.

steps.name: Gallipoli
steps.page:
An Anglo-French naval attempt to force the Dardanelles failed in March 1915, and troops were landed on the Gallipoli peninsula on 25 April to take the straits from the land. Ottoman forces held the high ground above the beaches, and the campaign settled into trench fighting as static as the Western Front.

The Allies evacuated in December 1915 and January 1916 without having advanced beyond their landing areas. Around half a million casualties were suffered on the two sides; the campaign is a founding memory in Australia, New Zealand and Turkey alike.

steps.name: The United States enters
steps.page:
Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February 1917, accepting American belligerency as the price of starving Britain out before it took effect. The Zimmermann telegram, in which Berlin offered Mexico an alliance and the recovery of its lost territories, was intercepted and published in March.

Congress declared war on 6 April 1917. American troops arrived slowly, about 175,000 by the end of the year but over a million by mid-1918, and the certainty of their arrival shaped both sides' plans for the following year.

steps.name: Russia leaves the war
steps.page:
The [Bolsheviks](item:october-revolution) took power in November 1917 committed to ending the war, and signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk on 3 March 1918. Russia gave up Poland, the Baltic provinces, Finland and Ukraine, a third of its population and much of its industry and grain.

The treaty freed some fifty German divisions for the Western Front and was annulled by the armistice in the west eight months later.

steps.name: The German spring offensive
steps.page:
Germany attacked on 21 March 1918 with divisions brought from the east, using short hurricane bombardments and infantry trained to infiltrate rather than to advance in line. The British Fifth Army was driven back some 60 km in a week, the deepest advance in the west since 1914, and further offensives followed in Flanders and on the Aisne.

The attacks took ground but not the railway junctions they needed, and cost about a million casualties the German army could not replace. The last of them was stopped on the Marne in July.

steps.name: The Hundred Days and the armistice
steps.page:
The Allied counter-offensive opened at Amiens on 8 August 1918 with tanks, aircraft and predicted artillery fire, and did not stop. Through the autumn the German army was pushed back off the Hindenburg Line while Bulgaria, the Ottoman Empire and Austria-Hungary left the war in turn.

Mutiny in the German fleet at Kiel spread into revolution; the Kaiser abdicated on 9 November. The armistice was signed in a railway carriage at Compiègne and took effect at 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918.

name: Russian Revolution
summary: Tsarism fell and the Bolsheviks built the world's first communist state.
body:
The Russian Revolution was the collapse of the Russian monarchy in 1917 and the seizure of power by the Bolsheviks eight months later, followed by a civil war that they won. It produced the world's first state governed by a communist party, which in 1922 became the [Soviet Union](event:ussr-founded).

Three years of [war](event:ww1) had cost Russia millions of casualties and wrecked the supply of food and fuel to its cities. In March 1917 bread queues and strikes in Petrograd turned into a general revolt that the garrison refused to put down, and Nicholas II abdicated. Power was then shared uneasily between a Provisional Government of liberals and moderate socialists and the soviets (councils of workers' and soldiers' deputies), which held the loyalty of the armed crowd.

The Provisional Government's decision to stay in the war destroyed it. Lenin, returned from exile in April, offered peace, land and bread and put the Bolsheviks in permanent opposition to it; a failed military intervention in September left the government without support on either side. On 7 November the Bolsheviks took Petrograd almost without a fight.

The new government made peace with Germany at Brest-Litovsk, dissolved the elected Constituent Assembly after a single day, nationalised industry and land, and met resistance with a political police. Civil war followed against White armies, nationalist governments and foreign expeditionary forces; it killed several million people, most of them by hunger and typhus rather than by fighting, and the Bolsheviks won it by 1922.

[Communist](event:communist-manifesto) parties elsewhere took the Bolshevik party as their model, and relations between the Soviet state and the Western powers became the [Cold War](event:cold-war) after 1945.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Revolution).

steps.name: The February Revolution
steps.page:
Strikes and bread riots in Petrograd on 8 March 1917 (International Women's Day, and 23 February in the old Russian calendar) grew within days into a general rising. The regiments of the city garrison sent to disperse the crowds mutinied and joined them.

The Duma formed a Provisional Government while the reconstituted Petrograd Soviet claimed the loyalty of the soldiers. Nicholas II abdicated on 15 March, and his brother refused the throne the next day; three centuries of Romanov rule ended in a week.

steps.name: Dual power
steps.page:
Through the spring and summer the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet governed against each other, the one with legal authority, the other with the garrison and the railways. Lenin returned from Switzerland in April demanding an immediate peace, land to the peasants and all power to the soviets.

The government chose instead to honour its commitments to the Allies and launched an offensive in June, which collapsed. Armed demonstrations in Petrograd in July (the July Days) were put down, Lenin fled to Finland, and Alexander Kerensky became prime minister.

steps.name: The Kornilov affair
steps.page:
In September 1917 the commander-in-chief, Lavr Kornilov, moved troops towards Petrograd. Whether he was acting with Kerensky's agreement against the left or against the government itself is still disputed; Kerensky dismissed him and appealed to the Soviet for defence.

Railwaymen stopped the trains and agitators talked the advancing units apart, and the affair ended in four days without fighting. It destroyed what credit the government had left with the officer corps, and the Bolsheviks, released from prison and armed to meet the threat, emerged from it with a majority in the Petrograd Soviet.

steps.name: The Civil War
steps.page:
The Bolsheviks held the centre (Petrograd, Moscow and the railways between them) against White armies in Siberia, the south and the north-west, nationalist governments in Ukraine, the Caucasus and the Baltic, peasant risings, and British, French, American and Japanese expeditionary forces.

Trotsky built the Red Army from conscripts and former tsarist officers; grain was requisitioned from the villages to feed the towns. Several million people died, the great majority of typhus, hunger and reprisal rather than in battle. The last White forces left Vladivostok in October 1922.

steps.name: Kronstadt and the New Economic Policy
steps.page:
In March 1921 the sailors of the Kronstadt naval base, who had been among the most reliable supporters of the revolution, rose against the government demanding free soviets and an end to grain requisitioning. The rising was crushed across the ice within a fortnight.

At the same congress the party abandoned the requisitioning that had provoked it. The New Economic Policy allowed private trade and small enterprise while the state kept heavy industry, banking and foreign trade, and the economy recovered from a famine that had killed some five million people.

name: Spanish flu pandemic
summary: An H1N1 influenza pandemic infected perhaps a third of humanity and killed tens of millions.
body:
The influenza pandemic of 1918–1920 was caused by an H1N1 virus and is the deadliest pandemic of the twentieth century. It infected around 500 million people, about a third of the world's population, and estimates of the dead range from 17 million to over 100 million; 25 to 50 million is the figure usually quoted.

The virus was unusual in whom it killed. Ordinary influenza is most dangerous to infants and the old; this one killed healthy adults between about twenty and forty in very large numbers, probably by provoking an overwhelming immune response in the lungs.

The pandemic is called the Spanish flu because of wartime censorship. Spain was neutral in the [First World War](event:ww1) and reported its epidemic freely, while the warring states suppressed the news to protect morale, so the outbreak appeared to belong to Spain. The earliest documented cases were in Kansas in early 1918. Troop trains, crowded camps and the movement of armies carried it around the world in months.

There were no vaccines, no antivirals and no antibiotics for the pneumonia that killed most victims. The measures that worked were the ones available in 1918: isolation, quarantine, closing schools and public gatherings, and banning mass meetings. Cities that acted early and kept the restrictions in place had markedly lower death rates.

The pandemic came in waves, and they are set out in the steps below.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_flu).

steps.name: The first wave
steps.page:
The first recognised outbreak ran through the spring and early summer of 1918. It spread very fast in army camps and in the ports and railways feeding the [Western Front](item:ww1), but killed at close to ordinary influenza rates, and in several countries it was recorded as a mild three-day fever.

By the summer it had reached most of Europe, North America and India, and had died away in many places. It left behind an infected population on both sides of a war that was moving millions of men between continents.

steps.name: The second wave
steps.page:
The second wave began in August 1918 and was far deadlier, killing within days through a viral pneumonia that could turn a patient blue for lack of oxygen. October 1918 was the worst month of the pandemic almost everywhere it reached.

Hospitals and undertakers were overwhelmed; some cities banned public gatherings and closed schools, theatres and churches, and the places that did so early and for long enough recorded markedly lower mortality. Most of the deaths of the whole pandemic fell in these four months.

steps.name: The third wave
steps.page:
A third wave ran from January to the late spring of 1919, less lethal than the second but heavy in Britain, Spain, Serbia, Mexico and Australia, which its quarantine had held off until then.

It reached the Paris peace conference: Woodrow Wilson fell seriously ill with influenza in April 1919 in the middle of the negotiation of the [Treaty of Versailles](item:versailles).

steps.name: The fourth wave
steps.page:
A final wave through the winter of 1919–20 struck parts of Europe, the United States and Japan. It was milder again, and by the spring of 1920 the pandemic had faded as the surviving population's immunity spread.

Descendants of the 1918 virus circulate still: every seasonal H1N1 influenza since, and the pandemics of 1957, 1968 and 2009, derive from it.

name: Great Depression
summary: The deepest economic collapse of the industrial age: a quarter of American workers unemployed, world trade down by two thirds.
body:
The Great Depression was the worldwide economic collapse of the 1930s, the deepest and longest of the industrial age. It began in the United States around the [Wall Street crash](event:wall-street-crash) of October 1929 and spread through trade and the gold standard to almost every country. American output fell by about a third and unemployment reached roughly a quarter of the workforce; world trade fell by around two thirds.

There is no single agreed cause. Contemporary weaknesses included an American boom financed by credit and stock speculation, agricultural prices already depressed through the 1920s, war debts and reparations that made international payments fragile, and banks with no deposit insurance and little supervision. The downturn deepened with the response to it: central banks defended the gold standard with high interest rates when the economy needed the opposite, thousands of banks failed and destroyed the credit and savings behind them, and the Smoot-Hawley tariff of 1930 helped set off a round of retaliation that shrank trade further.

Recovery came earliest to the countries that left gold first and could then loosen money (Britain in 1931, the United States in 1933). In the United States, Roosevelt's New Deal brought bank regulation, deposit insurance, public works, farm price support and, in 1935, social security. It did not end the slump, which returned in 1937–38 and was finished by rearmament and [war](event:ww2).

The Depression discredited liberal economics, expanded what states were expected to do for their citizens, and gave authoritarian movements their opening in Europe and Japan, in Germany above all, where the Nazi vote rose with unemployment and [Hitler took power](event:hitler-chancellor) in 1933.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression).

steps.name: The banking panics
steps.page:
Waves of bank failures ran through the United States from the autumn of 1930: the collapse of the Bank of United States in New York that December, further panics in 1931 and 1932, and a final one in the winter of 1932–33 in which states closed their banks one after another.

Around 9,000 banks failed. There was no deposit insurance, so their depositors simply lost their savings, and the credit that surviving banks would extend contracted with them. The money supply fell by about a third between 1929 and 1933. Later economists identified that contraction as the mechanism that turned a recession into a depression.

steps.name: Britain leaves gold
steps.page:
The failure of Austria's Creditanstalt in May 1931 set off a banking crisis across central Europe and a run on sterling. On 21 September Britain suspended the gold standard and let the pound float; it fell by about a quarter.

Two dozen countries followed within a year. Leaving gold freed a government to lower interest rates and expand credit instead of defending a fixed exchange rate, and the countries that left earliest recovered earliest, one of the clearest findings in the economic history of the Depression.

steps.name: The bank holiday and the New Deal
steps.page:
Roosevelt took office on 4 March 1933 with the banking system closed in most states. He declared a national bank holiday two days later, and Congress passed emergency legislation allowing sound banks to reopen under federal inspection; when they did, deposits came back.

The hundred days that followed created deposit insurance, securities regulation, farm price support, the Tennessee Valley Authority and public works and relief employment on a large scale. The United States left the gold standard in April. The New Deal did not end the Depression, but it stopped the collapse and rebuilt the machinery of finance.

steps.name: The recession of 1937
steps.page:
By 1937 output was approaching its 1929 level, and the administration cut spending to balance the budget while the Federal Reserve raised bank reserve requirements. The economy fell back sharply: industrial production dropped by about a third in nine months and unemployment rose again by several million.

Spending resumed in 1938 and the recovery with it. Full employment returned only with war orders. The sequence was later read as evidence for the argument John Maynard Keynes published in 1936.

name: World War II
summary: The deadliest conflict in history: some 70–85 million dead, fought across every ocean and most continents.
body:
World War II was fought from 1939 to 1945 between the Allies (chiefly the Soviet Union, the United States, Britain and China) and the Axis powers of Germany, Japan and Italy. It was the deadliest conflict in history: estimates of the dead run from 70 to 85 million, most of them civilians, killed in bombing, massacre, famine, disease and genocide as well as in battle.

The war in Europe began when Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939 and Britain and France declared war two days later. In Asia, Japan had been at war in [China](event:sino-japanese-war) since 1937. Germany overran Denmark, Norway, the Low Countries and France in the spring of 1940, failed to win the air battle over [Britain](event:battle-britain) that summer, and then turned east: [Operation Barbarossa](event:barbarossa) opened the largest land campaign ever fought on 22 June 1941. Japan's attack on [Pearl Harbor](event:pearl-harbor) in December brought the United States in, and Germany declared war on it four days later.

The Axis reached its furthest extent in 1942 and lost the initiative that autumn and winter at [Midway](event:midway), at El Alamein and at [Stalingrad](event:stalingrad). From then the war was a matter of Allied industrial weight and manpower closing in from three directions: the Red Army westward, the British and American armies through North Africa, Italy and then [Normandy](event:d-day), and the American advance across the Pacific. Strategic bombing destroyed the cities of Germany and Japan.

Behind the German front, the occupation regime carried out the [Holocaust](event:holocaust), murdering six million Jews, and killed millions more Soviet prisoners, Poles, Roma and disabled people. Japanese occupation forces killed on a comparable scale in China and South-East Asia.

Germany surrendered on 8 May 1945, weeks after Soviet troops took Berlin. Japan surrendered after the [atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki](event:hiroshima), the first use of the weapon the [Trinity test](event:trinity) had proved a month earlier, and the Soviet declaration of war in Manchuria; the formal surrender was signed on 2 September 1945.

The war left the United States and the Soviet Union as the only great powers, divided Europe between them for forty years in the [Cold War](event:cold-war), produced the United Nations, and broke the hold of the European empires on Asia and Africa.

The steps below follow the war from Britain's air defence to the Japanese surrender.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II).
